/conditions/cc.title: Condition Documentation Cards — CCs
/conditions/cc.html:
---

Hyponatremia

Classification: CC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

A sodium of 128 is a lab value. Hyponatremia is a diagnosis. If you ordered a sodium restriction, fluid restriction, or hypertonic saline — you diagnosed and treated hyponatremia. Write it.

Document This

✅ "Hyponatremia, sodium 124, likely SIADH in the setting of pneumonia. Free water restriction initiated."

✅ "Severe hyponatremia, Na 118, with neurological symptoms. Hypertonic saline infusion started, nephrology consulted."

✅ "Hyponatremia, hypervolemic, in the setting of decompensated heart failure. Diuresis initiated."

Not This

❌ "Na 128 — continue monitoring." — Lab value. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Low sodium, likely dilutional." — Clinical interpretation without a diagnosis.

❌ "Electrolyte abnormality." — Unspecified. Not codeable as hyponatremia.

Rules

  • Specify the type when known: hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH), or hypervolemic.
  • Severe hyponatremia with neurological symptoms (seizure, coma, obtundation) carries higher severity weight — document symptoms when present.
  • Hyponatremia is distinct from hypernatremia — both are CCs and should be documented separately when both occur.

Hypernatremia

Classification: CC

Applies to: SHFFT · Major Bowel · Any patient with impaired free water access

TEAM Pearl

Elderly, cognitively impaired, and postoperative patients are at high risk for hypernatremia. If sodium is consistently above 145 and you are managing it — document the diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Hypernatremia, sodium 152, likely due to insensible losses and reduced free water intake. Hypotonic IV fluids started."

✅ "Hypernatremia in the setting of central diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin initiated."

Not This

❌ "Sodium elevated — increase free water." — Order placed, diagnosis not documented.

❌ "Dehydration." — Dehydration is a symptom. Hypernatremia is the specific metabolic diagnosis.

Rules

  • Link to etiology when known: insufficient intake, excessive losses (GI, renal, insensible), diabetes insipidus.
  • Document treatment: free water replacement, hypotonic fluids, correction rate.

Metabolic Acidosis / Alkalosis

Classification: CC

Applies to: Major Bowel · CABG · SHFFT

TEAM Pearl

Arterial blood gases are ordered because you suspected an acid-base problem. If the results confirmed it and you treated it — document the diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Metabolic acidosis, anion gap 22, likely lactic acidosis in the setting of sepsis. Bicarbonate trending."

✅ "Metabolic alkalosis secondary to prolonged NG suction and volume contraction. Chloride replacement initiated."

✅ "Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis in the setting of hepatic failure."

Not This

❌ "ABG showing pH 7.28, bicarb 14 — continue monitoring." — Abnormal values documented, diagnosis not written.

❌ "Lactic acid elevated." — Lab finding. Lactic acidosis is the diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify type: metabolic vs. respiratory, acidosis vs. alkalosis.
  • Link to etiology: lactic acidosis from sepsis or ischemia, hyperchloremic acidosis from saline, contraction alkalosis from diuresis.
  • Mixed disorders — when both metabolic and respiratory components are present — should be documented as such.

Pleural Effusion

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · Major Bowel · Any patient with prolonged hospitalization

TEAM Pearl

Pleural effusion develops predictably after CABG and in many critically ill patients. It is imaged, it is often drained, and it is almost never documented as a diagnosis. If you ordered a thoracentesis or saw it on imaging and it changed management — write it.

Document This

✅ "Bilateral pleural effusions, moderate, post-CABG. Thoracentesis performed on the right, 800mL exudative fluid removed."

✅ "Pleural effusion, left-sided, contributing to respiratory compromise. Thoracentesis planned."

✅ "Small bilateral pleural effusions, clinically insignificant, noted on CXR. No intervention at this time." — Even when not treated, document it if it's clinically noted.

Not This

❌ "CXR with blunting of costophrenic angles." — Radiographic description. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Fluid overload with pulmonary changes." — Does not capture pleural effusion specifically.

Rules

  • Specify laterality: left, right, bilateral.
  • Specify size when known: small, moderate, large.
  • Specify if exudative vs. transudative when thoracentesis has been performed.
  • Link to etiology when known: post-CABG, heart failure, malignancy, pneumonia.

Ileus

Classification: CC

Applies to: Major Bowel · Any abdominal surgery

TEAM Pearl

NG tube placement, NPO status, and prolonged absence of bowel function are treatments. Ileus is the diagnosis. If you placed an NG tube for decompression — you diagnosed and treated ileus. Write it.

Document This

✅ "Postoperative ileus — absent bowel sounds, abdominal distension, NG tube output 1,200mL/day. NPO, decompression ongoing."

✅ "Prolonged ileus following sigmoid colectomy, day 5. KUB showing dilated loops without obstruction. Conservative management continued."

Not This

❌ "Slow GI recovery — NPO, NG tube in place." — Clinical situation documented, diagnosis not.

❌ "Not tolerating diet." — Symptom. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Abdominal distension." — Finding. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Distinguish ileus from small bowel obstruction — KUB or CT findings help; document which is present.
  • Postoperative ileus is expected after bowel surgery but still warrants documentation when it prolongs the stay or requires intervention.
  • Prolonged ileus (beyond the expected 2–3 days) is more clinically significant and should be clearly named.

Peritonitis

Classification: CC (when secondary to the procedure or as comorbidity) · MCC (when it is the primary driver of sepsis)

Applies to: Major Bowel

TEAM Pearl

When a bowel perforation causes peritonitis and sepsis, the peritonitis is part of what makes the case severe. Document it explicitly — not just the perforation.

Document This

✅ "Feculent peritonitis secondary to sigmoid perforation. Source control achieved with Hartmann's procedure. Broad-spectrum antibiotics continued."

✅ "Loculated peritonitis, right lower quadrant, from perforated appendix. Drainage and washout performed."

Not This

❌ "Perforated sigmoid — taken to OR." — Perforation documented, peritonitis not.

❌ "Abdominal contamination intraoperatively." — Operative finding, not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Link peritonitis to source: perforated diverticulitis, anastomotic leak, perforated peptic ulcer.
  • Specify type when known: feculent, bilious, purulent, loculated.
  • When peritonitis is the source of sepsis, document sepsis separately with peritonitis as the source.

C. difficile Infection

Classification: CC

Applies to: Major Bowel · Any prolonged antibiotic course

TEAM Pearl

A positive C. diff toxin is a lab result. C. difficile colitis is a diagnosis. If you started fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin — you treated a C. diff infection. Document it.

Document This

✅ "C. difficile colitis, confirmed on stool toxin PCR. Oral vancomycin started. Contact precautions in place."

✅ "Recurrent C. difficile infection — second episode within 3 months. Fidaxomicin initiated."

✅ "Severe C. difficile colitis with ileus and leukocytosis 28k. GI and surgery consulted."

Not This

❌ "C. diff positive — starting vanco." — Treatment started, diagnosis not documented.

❌ "Diarrhea, C. diff being ruled out." — Pending diagnosis. Document once confirmed.

Rules

  • Specify severity when applicable: non-severe, severe (WBC >15k or creatinine >1.5× baseline), or fulminant (hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon).
  • Recurrent episodes should be documented as recurrent — affects treatment decisions and coding.
  • Contact precautions should be documented — implies confirmed infection.

DVT (Acute)

Classification: CC

Applies to: LEJR · SHFFT · Spinal Fusion · Any procedure with VTE risk

TEAM Pearl

DVT prophylaxis is ordered for patients at risk. DVT treatment is ordered when it occurs. If you switched from prophylactic to therapeutic anticoagulation — that transition implies a DVT diagnosis. Document it.

Document This

✅ "Acute deep vein thrombosis, right popliteal vein, confirmed on duplex ultrasound. Therapeutic anticoagulation initiated."

✅ "Acute proximal DVT, left femoral-popliteal. Hematology consulted regarding anticoagulation in the setting of recent surgery."

Not This

❌ "DVT prophylaxis — Lovenox." — Prophylaxis is not treatment of a DVT.

❌ "Concern for DVT — duplex ordered." — Suspected diagnosis. Document once confirmed.

❌ "Leg swelling, ultrasound negative." — If negative, correctly not documented as DVT.

Rules

  • Specify location: proximal (femoral, iliac, popliteal) vs. distal (tibial, peroneal). Proximal carries higher clinical significance.
  • Specify laterality.
  • Distinguish acute from chronic — chronic DVT codes differently and carries less severity weight.
  • PE and DVT occurring together should both be documented.

Atelectasis

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · Major Bowel · Spinal Fusion — any procedure with prolonged anesthesia

TEAM Pearl

Atelectasis is the most common pulmonary complication after major surgery and one of the most consistently underdocumented. If you ordered incentive spirometry, chest PT, or bronchoscopy for mucus plugging — the clinical picture likely supports atelectasis.

Document This

✅ "Atelectasis, right lower lobe, post-CABG. Chest physiotherapy and incentive spirometry initiated. Respiratory therapy following."

✅ "Significant atelectasis with lobar collapse, left lower lobe. Bronchoscopy performed for mucus plug clearance."

Not This

❌ "CXR with basilar haziness." — Radiographic finding. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Incentive spirometry ordered." — Treatment. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify location when known: right lower lobe, bilateral basilar, left lower lobe.
  • Significant atelectasis with lobar collapse or requiring bronchoscopy is more clinically meaningful and should be documented with that detail.
  • Distinguish atelectasis from pneumonia when both are possible — the distinction affects code assignment and clinical clarity.

Hypertensive Crisis / Accelerated Hypertension

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · LEJR · Any procedure in a hypertensive patient

TEAM Pearl

Routine postoperative hypertension is expected and not a diagnosis. Hypertensive urgency (severe elevation without end-organ damage) and hypertensive emergency (severe elevation with end-organ damage) are diagnoses. If you gave IV antihypertensives or called cardiology — document why.

Document This

✅ "Hypertensive urgency — BP 198/112 persistent despite oral medications. IV labetalol given, blood pressure controlled."

✅ "Hypertensive emergency with acute hypertensive encephalopathy. Nicardipine drip initiated, neurology consulted."

✅ "Accelerated hypertension, BP consistently above 180/100 perioperatively. Antihypertensive regimen adjusted."

Not This

❌ "Hypertension — BP elevated, continue home meds." — Stable chronic hypertension. Not a hypertensive crisis.

❌ "BP 195/110 — gave hydralazine." — Treatment documented, diagnosis not.

Rules

  • Routine hypertension in a known hypertensive patient is not a crisis.
  • Hypertensive urgency = BP typically >180/120 without end-organ damage.
  • Hypertensive emergency = severe BP with end-organ damage: encephalopathy, acute MI, dissection, acute HF, AKI.
  • Document the specific end-organ effect when present — it affects both code assignment and clinical management.

Cellulitis

Classification: CC

Applies to: LEJR · SHFFT · Any surgical patient with wound complication

TEAM Pearl

Wound redness and warmth are findings. Cellulitis is a diagnosis. If you started antibiotics for a wound infection — document the diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Cellulitis, right lower extremity, extending 4cm beyond wound margins. Oral cephalexin started."

✅ "Postoperative wound cellulitis, left hip incision site, erythema and induration. IV antibiotics initiated given failure of oral therapy."

Not This

❌ "Wound redness — antibiotics started." — Finding plus treatment. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Surgical site infection concern." — Concern is not a diagnosis. Document once you have made the clinical determination.

Rules

  • Specify site and laterality.
  • Distinguish cellulitis from surgical site infection (SSI) — SSI has specific CDC criteria and HAC implications for certain procedures.
  • Severity matters: cellulitis requiring IV antibiotics vs. oral antibiotics is clinically and documentarily different.
  • For orthopedic patients, document whether infection is superficial (above fascia) or deep (below fascia, involving joint) — the distinction affects coding and clinical management significantly.

Osteomyelitis

Classification: CC

Applies to: LEJR · Spinal Fusion · Any procedure with bone involvement

TEAM Pearl

Osteomyelitis is a specific diagnosis that requires explicit physician documentation. "Bone infection" or "infected hardware" is not codeable without naming osteomyelitis or a specific infectious diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Acute osteomyelitis, left proximal femur, confirmed on MRI and bone biopsy — Staphylococcus aureus. IV vancomycin initiated, orthopedics and infectious disease co-managing."

✅ "Chronic osteomyelitis, lumbar spine (L4), with sinus tract formation. Surgical debridement planned."

Not This

❌ "Bone infection — cultures pending." — Document once confirmed.

❌ "Infected hardware." — Describes the clinical situation, not the diagnosis. Osteomyelitis and periprosthetic joint infection are distinct diagnoses.

Rules

  • Specify acute vs. chronic.
  • Specify site and organism when known.
  • Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a distinct diagnosis from osteomyelitis — use the appropriate term for the clinical picture.
  • Vertebral osteomyelitis in the spinal fusion population should be documented with level, organism, and whether hardware is involved.

Cardiomyopathy (Non-Ischemic)

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · LEJR · Any patient with reduced EF

TEAM Pearl

Reduced ejection fraction without a named underlying cause codes as heart failure — not cardiomyopathy. If the patient has dilated cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or another specified type, name it alongside the heart failure diagnosis. Both conditions code separately.

Document This

✅ "Dilated cardiomyopathy, non-ischemic, EF 25%. Managed with guideline-directed medical therapy."

✅ "Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy — gradient 45mmHg on echo, on metoprolol."

✅ "Peripartum cardiomyopathy, EF recovering from nadir of 20%. Current EF 38%."

Not This

❌ "Poor EF — continue cardiac meds." — EF noted, cardiomyopathy diagnosis not written.

❌ "Cardiomegaly on CXR." — Radiographic finding. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify type: dilated, hypertrophic (obstructive vs. non-obstructive), restrictive, arrhythmogenic, peripartum, stress (Takotsubo).
  • Ischemic cardiomyopathy (caused by CAD) codes from the ischemic heart disease category — it is distinct from non-ischemic cardiomyopathy.
  • Document EF when available — supports clinical validity.
  • Both cardiomyopathy and heart failure should be coded when both are present.

Coagulopathy (Non-DIC)

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · Major Bowel · SHFFT — patients on anticoagulants or with liver disease

TEAM Pearl

Coagulopathy in the context of liver disease, massive transfusion, or anticoagulant therapy is a documentable diagnosis. "PT/PTT elevated" is a lab value. If the coagulopathy changed your management — it needs a name.

Document This

✅ "Coagulopathy secondary to hepatic dysfunction — INR 3.2, FFP administered preoperatively."

✅ "Acquired coagulopathy in the setting of massive transfusion. Ratio-based resuscitation protocol initiated."

✅ "Coagulopathy due to warfarin — supratherapeutic INR 6.1. Vitamin K administered, held warfarin."

Not This

❌ "INR elevated — FFP given." — Lab value and treatment. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Patient on blood thinners." — Medication documentation, not a coagulopathy diagnosis.

Rules

  • Link to etiology: liver disease, medications, dilutional, massive transfusion, vitamin K deficiency.
  • Distinguish from DIC — DIC has its own higher-severity code and criteria.
  • Document the INR or PT/PTT level in context with the diagnosis for audit support.

Malnutrition (Moderate)

Classification: CC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

If the patient isn't severely malnourished — they may still be moderately malnourished. Moderate malnutrition is a CC. When you can't reach severe, reach for moderate. Both require physician documentation. Neither requires the dietitian to do it for you.

Document This

✅ "Moderate protein-calorie malnutrition — 7% weight loss over 3 months, mild muscle wasting on exam, reduced intake in setting of chronic illness. Consistent with ASPEN criteria for moderate malnutrition. Oral nutritional supplements initiated."

✅ "Moderate malnutrition in the context of active malignancy — reduced intake, early satiety, mild-moderate muscle loss. Dietitian-guided nutrition plan in place."

Not This

❌ "Nutritional deficiency — dietitian following." — Not a physician diagnosis.

❌ "Patient eating poorly." — Observation. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Moderate malnutrition = CC. Severe malnutrition = MCC. The distinction requires physician documentation of severity.
  • ASPEN criteria: at least 2 of the following in the context of illness — energy deficit, weight loss (moderate: 5% in 1 month or 10% in 6 months), muscle wasting, fat wasting, fluid accumulation, reduced grip strength.
  • When the clinical picture is borderline between moderate and severe, document your clinical reasoning for the severity determination.
  • Even mild malnutrition (unspecified) captures a CC — better than no nutrition diagnosis at all.

Acute Pancreatitis

Classification: MCC (acute) · CC (chronic)

Applies to: Major Bowel

TEAM Pearl

Acute pancreatitis severity should be documented. Mild pancreatitis is not an MCC. Severe acute pancreatitis with organ failure is. The distinction is clinically important and documentarily impactful.

Document This

✅ "Acute pancreatitis, mild, likely gallstone etiology. NPO, IV fluids, pain management. Lipase 1,840."

✅ "Severe acute pancreatitis with acute kidney injury and respiratory failure — organ failure present. ICU admission, nutrition via NJ tube."

✅ "Necrotizing pancreatitis — CT showing >30% pancreatic necrosis. Interventional radiology and surgery consulted."

Not This

❌ "Elevated lipase — pancreatitis?" — Query framing. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Abdominal pain, lipase elevated." — Symptom and lab. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify severity: mild (no organ failure), moderately severe (transient organ failure), severe (persistent organ failure >48h).
  • Specify etiology when known: gallstone, alcohol, hypertriglyceridemia, medication-induced, idiopathic.
  • Necrotizing pancreatitis and infected pancreatic necrosis are distinct, higher-severity diagnoses that should be named explicitly when present.
  • Chronic pancreatitis = CC; acute pancreatitis = MCC.

Hemiplegia / Hemiparesis

Classification: CC

Applies to: SHFFT · LEJR — patients with prior stroke

TEAM Pearl

Patients with prior stroke often have residual motor deficits that directly affect surgical risk, rehabilitation potential, and post-acute planning. Documenting "history of stroke" captures the prior event but not the active functional deficit. The deficit is what codes as a CC.

Document This

✅ "Left hemiparesis — residual motor deficit from right MCA stroke 2 years ago. Baseline ambulation with hemi-walker. Present on admission."

✅ "Right hemiplegia following prior hemorrhagic stroke. Fully dependent for transfers. Affects surgical planning and rehab disposition."

Not This

❌ "History of stroke, left-sided weakness." — History of codes as resolved event. Weakness is a symptom. Neither captures the CC.

❌ "CVA in past." — Prior event only. No functional deficit documented.

Rules

  • Document the active functional deficit — hemiplegia (complete) or hemiparesis (partial) — not just the prior event.
  • Specify side: left vs. right.
  • Establish that the deficit is present on admission — relevant for POA status.
  • Document functional baseline: ambulation status, transfer status, grip strength — supports the clinical picture.

Schizophrenia

Classification: CC

Applies to: Any procedure in a patient with serious mental illness

TEAM Pearl

Schizophrenia is one of the most consistent predictors of complicated hospital courses, longer length of stay, and higher readmission risk. It is also consistently underdocumented in surgical patients. If it is active and being managed — document it.

Document This

✅ "Schizophrenia, paranoid type, stable on risperidone. Continued home antipsychotic during hospitalization. Psychiatry consulted for behavioral management."

✅ "Schizoaffective disorder — home quetiapine continued. Behavioral health team involved in discharge planning."

Not This

❌ "Psychiatric history." — Not a diagnosis. Not codeable.

❌ "On antipsychotics." — Medication without diagnosis.

❌ "Schizophrenia — history." — History framing implies resolved. Schizophrenia is a chronic active condition.

Rules

  • Specify type when known: paranoid, disorganized, catatonic, undifferentiated, schizoaffective.
  • Document that it is active and currently managed.
  • Continuing home antipsychotics during hospitalization implies active diagnosis — write it.
  • Unspecified schizophrenia still codes as a CC — better than no diagnosis.

Condition Documentation Cards — CCs · TEAM Playbook

Last updated June 2026 · Reflects CMS MS-DRG V43.0 and ICD-10-CM FY2026

CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule

/conditions.title: Condition Documentation Cards
/conditions.html:
---

Sepsis

Classification: MCC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

Sepsis requires two things documented: an infection source and a systemic response causing organ dysfunction. "Infection" alone is not sepsis. "SIRS" alone is not sepsis. You must write both — and link them.

Document This

✅ "Sepsis due to gram-negative bacteremia, source urinary tract. Meeting Sepsis-3 criteria with acute kidney injury and hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation."

✅ "Severe sepsis with acute respiratory failure secondary to community-acquired pneumonia."

✅ "Septic shock — vasopressors required to maintain MAP ≥65 despite adequate resuscitation. Source: infected surgical wound."

Not This

❌ "Infection — antibiotics started." — Not sepsis. Will not be coded as sepsis.

❌ "Urosepsis." — Not a valid ICD-10 term. Will generate a query. Write sepsis due to UTI instead.

❌ "SIRS." — Not sepsis. Different diagnosis, different code, no MCC.

❌ "Sepsis workup ordered." — Unconfirmed; cannot be coded until the physician documents the diagnosis.

Rules

  • Name the source. "Sepsis" without a source codes correctly but is harder to defend.
  • For severe sepsis, name the organ dysfunction — AKI, respiratory failure, encephalopathy. "Multi-organ dysfunction" alone is insufficient for coding organ dysfunction.
  • For septic shock, document vasopressor requirement and persistent hypotension explicitly.
Denial Risk

Sepsis is the most audited diagnosis in inpatient medicine. Auditors look for: treatment consistent with sepsis (blood cultures, IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation), organ dysfunction documentation, and explicit physician attestation — not just nursing or respiratory therapy notes.

Acute Kidney Injury

Classification: MCC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

A rising creatinine is a lab value. Acute kidney injury is a diagnosis. You must write the diagnosis. KDIGO Stage 1 threshold: creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days.

Document This

✅ "Acute kidney injury, likely prerenal, creatinine 2.4 from baseline 1.0. IV fluids started, nephrotoxins held."

✅ "AKI with acute tubular necrosis, contrast-induced. Nephrology consulted."

✅ "Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease stage 3. Both conditions active and being managed."

Not This

❌ "Creatinine elevated, monitoring." — Lab finding. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Prerenal azotemia." — Not a valid coding term. Write AKI instead.

❌ "Creatinine up from baseline, likely related to contrast — will trend." — Still a lab observation, not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • When AKI occurs in a patient with CKD, document both — AKI and the CKD stage. Missing either loses severity.
  • ATN (acute tubular necrosis) should be specified when the mechanism supports it — contrast, ischemia, aminoglycosides, rhabdomyolysis.
  • Stage is not required in the note but is helpful for audit defense.
Denial Risk

Top RAC target. Auditors look for creatinine values meeting threshold, clinical response (IV fluids, held nephrotoxins, nephrology consult), and documentation throughout the stay — not only in the discharge summary.

Metabolic or Toxic Encephalopathy

Classification: MCC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

"Confusion" is a symptom. "Altered mental status" is a symptom. "Delirium" is a CC — not an MCC. Metabolic or toxic encephalopathy is an MCC. The etiology is what makes the diagnosis specific enough to code correctly.

Document This

✅ "Acute metabolic encephalopathy secondary to uremia and hyponatremia."

✅ "Toxic encephalopathy due to opioid toxicity."

✅ "Septic encephalopathy — metabolic encephalopathy in the setting of sepsis." (Septic encephalopathy codes as metabolic.)

✅ "Acute metabolic encephalopathy in the setting of chronic hepatic encephalopathy." — When both are present, document both explicitly.

Not This

❌ "Confusion, likely multifactorial." — Multifactorial is not codeable. Name the cause.

❌ "AMS — delirium precautions in place." — Delirium is a CC; encephalopathy is an MCC. If the clinical picture supports encephalopathy, document it.

❌ "Encephalopathy." — Without metabolic or toxic qualifier, codes to unspecified encephalopathy. Audit exposure.

Rules

  • Always classify as metabolic or toxic, or both. "Acute encephalopathy" alone is a less specific code.
  • Metabolic = internal cause (electrolyte, organ failure, sepsis, hypoxia).
  • Toxic = external cause (alcohol, medication, drug, toxin).
  • Link the etiology: "due to," "secondary to," "in the setting of."
Denial Risk

Heavily scrutinized. Auditors look for documented cognitive change from baseline, labs or findings consistent with the named etiology, and clinical response to treatment of the underlying cause.

Severe Malnutrition

Classification: MCC (severe) · CC (moderate or unspecified)

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

The dietitian can identify and document malnutrition findings. Only the physician can establish the diagnosis for coding purposes. A dietitian note alone — no matter how detailed — cannot be coded as a physician diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Severe protein-calorie malnutrition — greater than 10% weight loss over 2 months, significant muscle wasting on exam, energy intake less than 50% of estimated needs. Consistent with ASPEN criteria for severe malnutrition in the context of acute illness. TPN initiated."

✅ "Moderate malnutrition in the setting of chronic illness — reduced intake, mild muscle wasting, consistent with ASPEN criteria. Nutrition support initiated."

Not This

❌ "Poor appetite — dietary consult placed." — No diagnosis. Not codeable.

❌ "Low albumin." — Albumin is not a required criterion for malnutrition under current ASPEN or GLIM criteria and is not a diagnosis.

❌ "Cachectic." — Codes as cachexia, which is a CC but is not the same as malnutrition.

Rules

  • Severity matters: severe = MCC, moderate = CC, unspecified = CC. Document the severity.
  • Treatment must match severity. A patient documented as severely malnourished should have aggressive nutritional intervention — TPN, tube feeds, or equivalent. Mismatch triggers audits.
  • ASPEN criteria require at least 2 of: energy deficit, weight loss, muscle wasting, fat wasting, fluid accumulation, reduced grip strength — in the context of acute illness, chronic illness, or social circumstances.
Denial Risk

OIG priority. Auditors look for ASPEN/GLIM criteria support, physician documentation (not dietitian only), and treatment intensity consistent with stated severity.

Acute Heart Failure

Classification: MCC (acute or acute-on-chronic) · CC (chronic or unspecified)

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

"CHF" and "heart failure" written alone are unspecified diagnoses. Unspecified heart failure is not a CC or MCC. Three words fix it: acute, systolic or diastolic.

Document This

✅ "Acute on chronic systolic heart failure. IV diuresis initiated, 2L net negative. EF 35% on prior echo."

✅ "Acute diastolic heart failure, new onset. BNP 2,400, pulmonary edema on CXR, responding to IV Lasix."

✅ "Chronic systolic heart failure, stable. Continue home furosemide and carvedilol." — CC only, but still documented correctly.

Not This

❌ "CHF — gave Lasix." — Unspecified. No CC or MCC.

❌ "Heart failure exacerbation." — "Exacerbation" does not code to acute. Write acute explicitly.

❌ "Volume overloaded." — Clinical finding, not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify systolic vs. diastolic — or combined if both are present.
  • Specify acuity — acute, chronic, or acute-on-chronic.
  • Include EF when available. It does not change the code but supports audit defense.
  • If the patient received IV diuresis, the clinical picture almost always supports acute HF. Document it as such.

Acute Respiratory Failure

Classification: MCC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

Hypoxia is a finding. Respiratory distress is a symptom. Acute respiratory failure is a diagnosis. Mechanical ventilation is not required — patients on high-flow nasal cannula or BiPAP can qualify.

Document This

✅ "Acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula at 40L/60%. Likely pneumonia-related."

✅ "Acute hypercapnic respiratory failure due to COPD exacerbation. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation initiated."

✅ "Acute-on-chronic respiratory failure — baseline hypercapnia, now acutely worsening requiring BiPAP."

Not This

❌ "Hypoxia — supplemental O2 started." — Symptom and treatment. Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Respiratory distress, improving on O2." — Not a diagnosis.

❌ "Prolonged intubation." — Describes a treatment, not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify type: hypoxic (low O2), hypercapnic (high CO2), or both.
  • Link to etiology when known: pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary edema, sepsis.
  • If the patient required escalation beyond routine supplemental O2 — high-flow, BiPAP, CPAP, or intubation — the clinical picture likely supports respiratory failure. Document it.
Denial Risk

Auditors look for SpO2 or ABG values consistent with the diagnosis, escalation of respiratory support beyond routine O2, and documentation throughout the stay.

Acute Pulmonary Embolism

Classification: MCC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures (especially LEJR, SHFFT, Spinal Fusion)

TEAM Pearl

PE must be confirmed and diagnosed by the physician — a positive CT-PA is a finding, not a diagnosis. Write the diagnosis explicitly in the note.

Document This

✅ "Acute pulmonary embolism confirmed on CT-PA. Anticoagulation initiated with therapeutic enoxaparin."

✅ "Submassive pulmonary embolism with right heart strain on echo. Hematology consulted, systemic thrombolytics considered."

✅ "Acute bilateral pulmonary emboli, hemodynamically stable. Anticoagulation started."

Not This

❌ "CT-PA positive — starting heparin." — Positive finding documented, diagnosis not written.

❌ "Suspected PE, anticoagulated empirically." — Suspected is not codeable. Once confirmed, write the confirmed diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify acuity: acute vs. chronic. Chronic PE codes differently and carries less severity weight.
  • Massive (hemodynamic compromise) vs. submassive (right heart strain without shock) is clinically meaningful and should be documented when applicable.
  • POA matters for PE: a PE present on admission vs. one that develops during hospitalization affects HAC implications for orthopedic procedures specifically.

Acute Myocardial Infarction

Classification: MCC

Applies to: CABG · All five procedures when it occurs as a complication

TEAM Pearl

"Troponin elevation" is a lab value. "Demand ischemia" is a clinical finding. Acute myocardial infarction is a diagnosis. Perioperative MI after CABG is not "expected troponin release" — it is a codeable, documentable, MCC-generating diagnosis when the clinical criteria are met.

Document This

✅ "NSTEMI — troponin peak 18 ng/mL with new ST changes in leads V4-V6. Cardiology managing."

✅ "Perioperative myocardial infarction, type 5, post-CABG. New wall motion abnormality on echo, troponin significantly elevated above expected post-bypass range."

✅ "Acute STEMI, inferior wall. Emergent cath lab activation."

Not This

❌ "Troponin bump — expected after bypass." — Not a diagnosis. If criteria are met, document MI.

❌ "Demand ischemia." — CC only, not MCC. If the picture supports MI, document MI.

❌ "Elevated troponin, etiology unclear." — Uncertainty is acceptable — but once you have made a clinical determination, document it.

Rules

  • STEMI vs. NSTEMI: specify when known.
  • Perioperative MI (type 5) after CABG is its own category — document it separately from expected post-bypass troponin release when clinical criteria support it.
  • Type 2 MI (demand ischemia causing myocardial necrosis) is a higher-acuity diagnosis than demand ischemia alone — document when the clinical picture supports it.

Severe Sepsis / Septic Shock

Classification: MCC (if patient survives to discharge)

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

Note

Septic shock is a specific diagnosis distinct from sepsis. It requires both vasopressor dependence and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate resuscitation. Document both elements explicitly.

Document This

✅ "Septic shock — persistent hypotension requiring norepinephrine, lactate 4.2 mmol/L despite 3L IVF. Source: intra-abdominal infection."

✅ "Severe sepsis with acute organ dysfunction: AKI stage 2 and metabolic encephalopathy, in the setting of gram-positive bacteremia."

Not This

❌ "On pressors for hypotension." — Describes treatment, not diagnosis.

❌ "Sepsis, hypotensive." — Hypotension alone doesn't document shock. Write septic shock when vasopressors are required.

Rules

  • Septic shock = sepsis + vasopressors + lactate >2 despite resuscitation. All three elements should be evident in the chart.
  • Severe sepsis = sepsis + named organ dysfunction. Name the organ — AKI, respiratory failure, encephalopathy — don't just write "multi-organ dysfunction."
  • Both are MCC only if the patient is discharged alive.

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC)

Classification: MCC

Applies to: Major Bowel · CABG · SHFFT (sepsis-related DIC)

TEAM Pearl

DIC in the setting of sepsis or major surgery is frequently present and rarely documented. If the patient has thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated D-dimer, and fibrinogen dropping — and you are treating it — document the diagnosis.

Document This

✅ "Disseminated intravascular coagulation in the setting of septic shock — thrombocytopenia, elevated D-dimer, hypofibrinogenemia. FFP and cryoprecipitate administered."

✅ "DIC, acute, secondary to gram-negative sepsis. Hematology consulted."

Not This

❌ "Coagulopathy — FFP given." — Coagulopathy is a symptom. DIC is a diagnosis.

❌ "Labs consistent with DIC." — Labs support the diagnosis; the physician must state it.

Rules

  • Link DIC to its cause: sepsis, major surgery, malignancy, obstetric complication.
  • Treatment should match: FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelet transfusion, or hematology involvement supports the diagnosis clinically.

Pressure Ulcer (Stage III or IV)

Classification: MCC (Stage III or IV) · CC (Stage II)

Applies to: SHFFT · LEJR · Any immobilized patient

TEAM Pearl

Physicians must document the stage. Nursing documents the wound — but the physician's attestation of stage is required for coding. An unstaged pressure ulcer codes as unspecified — no CC or MCC.

Document This

✅ "Stage III sacral pressure injury, present on admission. Wound care team managing."

✅ "Stage IV right heel pressure ulcer with exposed tendon, developed during hospitalization." — Note: developed during hospitalization = HAC implications; POA = N.

✅ "Stage II left hip pressure injury, present on admission. Wound care initiated."

Not This

❌ "Decubitus ulcer — wound care ordered." — No stage. Codes as unspecified. No CC or MCC.

❌ "Redness to sacrum." — Stage I. Not a CC or MCC.

Rules

  • Stage the wound as the physician of record, not just nursing.
  • POA status is critical: Stage III/IV present on admission = MCC. Stage III/IV acquired during hospitalization = HAC — will not move the DRG tier.
  • Document site and laterality: sacral, right heel, left ischium, etc.

Aspiration Pneumonia

Classification: MCC

Applies to: SHFFT · Major Bowel · Any procedure with prolonged intubation

TEAM Pearl

Aspiration pneumonia and aspiration pneumonitis are different diagnoses with different codes. Aspiration pneumonia = bacterial infection from aspirated material. Aspiration pneumonitis = chemical inflammation from aspiration. The clinical picture and treatment determine which applies.

Document This

✅ "Aspiration pneumonia, right lower lobe, following witnessed aspiration event. IV antibiotics started."

✅ "Healthcare-associated pneumonia with suspected aspiration component in an intubated patient."

Not This

❌ "Aspiration event — monitoring." — Event documented, diagnosis not.

❌ "Pneumonia." — Specify type: aspiration, community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated. Each codes differently.

Rules

  • Aspiration pneumonia is an MCC. Standard pneumonia (without aspiration or viral specification) may code as MCC or CC depending on the organism.
  • For intubated patients, distinguish ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) from aspiration — VAP has HAC implications.
  • Document the side and lobe when known.

Atrial Fibrillation

Classification: CC

Applies to: CABG · LEJR · All procedures in elderly patients

TEAM Pearl

Atrial fibrillation is one of the most prevalent cardiac diagnoses in surgical patients and one of the most vaguely documented. "A-fib" codes correctly — but the type matters for clinical completeness and audit defense.

Document This

✅ "Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, converted to sinus rhythm with amiodarone. Discharged in sinus."

✅ "Persistent atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, rate controlled on metoprolol. Anticoagulated with apixaban."

✅ "New-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation, POD2 after CABG. Spontaneously converted. Amiodarone continued for 4 weeks."

Not This

❌ "Irregular rhythm." — Not codeable.

❌ "A-fib history." — History of codes as resolved. If active, document as active.

❌ "Rate-controlled." — Describes management, not diagnosis.

Rules

  • Specify type: paroxysmal (terminates spontaneously), persistent (requires intervention or ongoing), long-standing persistent, or permanent.
  • New post-operative AF in CABG patients is extremely common and almost as commonly underdocumented. Document it.
  • If present at admission, document as POA. If new during hospitalization, document when it started.

COPD with Acute Exacerbation

Classification: CC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

"COPD" alone codes correctly as a chronic diagnosis but without exacerbation it carries less severity weight. "COPD with acute exacerbation" is the CC. If you escalated treatment — added steroids, nebulizers, changed O2 requirements — document the exacerbation.

Document This

✅ "COPD with acute exacerbation — increased dyspnea, worsening airflow obstruction. Systemic steroids and scheduled nebulizers started."

✅ "Acute exacerbation of COPD requiring IV methylprednisolone and respiratory therapy."

Not This

❌ "COPD — continued home inhalers." — Stable COPD. No exacerbation captured.

❌ "Bronchospasm." — Symptom, not a diagnosis.

❌ "Wheezing, SOB — nebulizer treatments given." — Treatment documented, exacerbation diagnosis not.

Rules

  • Exacerbation means worsening from baseline requiring treatment escalation: steroids, increased bronchodilators, O2 change, or antibiotics for infectious exacerbation.
  • Link to infection if present: "COPD exacerbation with acute bronchitis due to H. influenzae."
  • If respiratory failure develops on top of COPD exacerbation, document both.

Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome

Classification: CC

Applies to: LEJR · SHFFT · Spinal Fusion — any procedure in morbidly obese patients on home CPAP/BiPAP

TEAM Pearl

"Morbid obesity" and "obstructive sleep apnea" are not OHS. OHS requires daytime hypercapnia — chronic CO2 retention while awake. If your patient uses home BiPAP and has a BMI over 35, OHS is likely and worth documenting.

Document This

✅ "Obesity hypoventilation syndrome — BMI 46, home BiPAP, prior ABG with daytime pCO₂ 52 mmHg. BiPAP continued perioperatively."

✅ "OHS (Pickwickian syndrome) — on home BiPAP, daytime hypercapnia documented on prior pulmonology workup."

Not This

❌ "Morbid obesity on CPAP for sleep apnea." — OSA and OHS are different diagnoses. OSA is not a CC. OHS is.

❌ "BMI 48, home CPAP." — BMI is a finding. OHS is a diagnosis.

Rules

  • OHS requires BMI ≥30 and awake daytime hypercapnia (pCO₂ >45 mmHg) not explained by another cause.
  • If prior ABG or pulmonology documentation supports the diagnosis, reference it.
  • "Pickwickian syndrome" is an accepted alternate term that codes identically.

Acute Blood Loss Anemia

Classification: CC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

When you order a transfusion, document why. "Postop anemia" codes as unspecified anemia — not a CC. "Acute blood loss anemia" is a CC and accurately reflects why the patient needed blood.

Document This

✅ "Acute blood loss anemia — hemoglobin 7.1 following 800mL estimated blood loss intraoperatively. Two units pRBC transfused."

✅ "Anemia of acute blood loss, postoperative. Hemoglobin dropped from 12.4 preoperatively to 7.8. Transfusion initiated."

Not This

❌ "Postop anemia — transfusion given." — Unspecified anemia. Not a CC.

❌ "Hemoglobin low — transfuse." — Lab finding plus order. Not a diagnosis.

Rules

  • "Acute blood loss anemia" (D62) is the correct term. It codes as a CC.
  • Iron deficiency anemia or anemia of chronic disease are different diagnoses — don't use those terms if the etiology is surgical blood loss.
  • Chronic anemia present before surgery codes separately from acute blood loss anemia that develops during or after the procedure. Document both if both are present.

Drug or Alcohol Withdrawal

Classification: CC

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

Patients who use alcohol or opioids daily will withdraw during hospitalization. "History of alcohol use" is not a diagnosis. Withdrawal is an active, manageable, codeable condition — and a common unexpected complication that CDI programs consistently flag as underdocumented.

Document This

✅ "Alcohol withdrawal syndrome, uncomplicated. CIWA protocol initiated, lorazepam administered."

✅ "Opioid withdrawal in setting of chronic opioid dependence — patient using 80mg oxycodone daily at home, now without access. Methadone/buprenorphine bridge started."

✅ "Alcohol withdrawal with seizure. Neurology consulted, benzodiazepine protocol escalated."

Not This

❌ "History of alcohol use, monitoring for withdrawal." — No diagnosis. Not codeable.

❌ "ETOH use disorder." — Use disorder alone is a different code than withdrawal. If withdrawal is occurring, document withdrawal.

Rules

  • Specify the substance: alcohol, opioid, benzodiazepine, etc.
  • Specify severity when applicable: uncomplicated, with seizure, with delirium (delirium tremens).
  • CIWA score initiation and benzodiazepine administration in the chart support the diagnosis clinically.

Dementia with Behavioral Disturbance

Classification: CC

Applies to: SHFFT · LEJR — elderly surgical patients

TEAM Pearl

"Dementia" alone codes as unspecified dementia. "Dementia with behavioral disturbance" is a CC. If the patient is agitated, wandering, aggressive, or has delusions on top of baseline dementia — document the behavioral disturbance.

Document This

✅ "Moderate Alzheimer's dementia with behavioral disturbance — agitation and combativeness, requiring redirection. On donepezil at home."

✅ "Vascular dementia with behavioral disturbance — sundowning, acute agitation in the evening. Quetiapine initiated."

Not This

❌ "Dementia — patient confused." — Unspecified dementia. No CC if behavioral disturbance not specified.

❌ "Known dementia, oriented to person only." — Orientation level noted, behavioral disturbance not named.

Rules

  • Specify dementia type when known: Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal.
  • Behavioral disturbance includes: agitation, aggression, wandering, psychosis, sundowning, combativeness.
  • Pre-fracture cognitive baseline should be documented for SHFFT patients — it distinguishes acute delirium from underlying dementia and matters for disposition planning.

Chronic Kidney Disease (Staged)

Classification: CC (Stage IV) · MCC (Stage V / ESRD)

Applies to: All five TEAM procedures

TEAM Pearl

"CKD" without a stage codes as unspecified and does not carry CC or MCC weight. The eGFR is in the chart. Stage the CKD.

Document This

✅ "Chronic kidney disease, stage 4 — eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m². Nephrology following."

✅ "End-stage renal disease on hemodialysis three times weekly."

✅ "CKD stage 3b — eGFR 34. Monitored, no dialysis yet."

Not This

❌ "CKD — creatinine at baseline." — Unspecified. No CC.

❌ "Renal insufficiency." — Vague. No codeable stage.

❌ "Chronic renal disease." — Unspecified. No CC.

Rules

StageeGFRClassification
3a45–59No CC/MCC
3b30–44No CC/MCC
415–29CC
5<15MCC
ESRDOn dialysisMCC
  • When AKI occurs on top of CKD, document both and stage both.
  • ESRD on dialysis is an MCC — document dialysis status and frequency explicitly.

/.title: TEAM Playbook
/.html:
Hero

Your documentation is worth more than you think.

Your hospital now receives a single bundled payment for each episode of care, and Medicare calculates this payment based on the severity of illness documented for your patients. The only way insurance companies can assess how sick the patients are is through the documentation you provide. This playbook outlines what this means in practice and offers guidance on what to write.

Role Selector

Who are you?

I'm a Surgeon

Your orders and your discharge summary are the two highest-leverage documents in the episode. Where you send a patient after surgery — home, SNF, or rehab — determines a large share of episode cost. What you write in the discharge summary determines whether your patient's clinical complexity is captured or invisible to the payment system.

This playbook tells you which diagnoses to name, how to phrase them, and what a compliant discharge summary looks like for each of the five procedures.

Start here → Your procedure's quick reference card. Five minutes before your next discharge.

I'm a Medicine Physician or Hospitalist

You manage the comorbidities. That makes you the most important documentation author in the building for TEAM purposes. Sepsis, AKI, encephalopathy, malnutrition, heart failure — the diagnoses that move DRG tiers are almost always documented (or missed) by medicine, not surgery.

This playbook tells you exactly which conditions to name, how specifically to name them, and why "CHF" and "confusion" are not diagnoses for coding purposes.

Start here → CDI Fundamentals, then the CC/MCC Reference. The phrasing examples are written for your notes, not surgical notes.

I'm an APP

You write progress notes and often the discharge summary. The discharge summary is the final opportunity to capture every diagnosis that was managed during the stay — and the one document coders rely on most. An incomplete or vague discharge summary leaves complexity uncaptured regardless of what appeared in earlier notes.

This playbook gives you the phrasing, the checklists, and the before/after examples you need to write a discharge summary that accurately reflects what happened.

Start here → The quick reference card for your procedure. Use the discharge checklist at the bottom of every card.

What This Is About — In 60 Seconds

Medicare now pays for joint replacements, hip fracture surgeries, bypass operations, spinal fusions, and bowel resections as bundled episodes. One payment covers the surgery, the hospital stay, and 30 days of care after discharge — including any readmissions, SNF stays, rehab, and home health.

That payment is set in advance based on a target price. Your hospital keeps the difference if total costs come in under target. Your hospital owes money if costs exceed target.

Two things directly affect that target price:

1. DRG tier. The severity tier of the anchor hospitalization is determined by secondary diagnoses — CCs and MCCs. "CHF" is not an MCC. "Acute systolic heart failure" is. Same clinical situation, different DRG, different payment, different episode performance.

2. HCC risk adjustment. Chronic conditions documented in the six months before surgery adjust the target price upward for complex patients. A patient with heart failure, COPD, and diabetes with neuropathy generates a higher target price than the same patient with no documented comorbidities — as long as those conditions are documented.

Neither of these requires documenting anything that isn't clinically present. Both require documenting what is present with enough precision for the coding system to represent it accurately.

That is the whole thing. That is what this playbook is for.

What's in This Playbook

Every section is a benefit statement, not a topic label.

Understand the TEAM Model

What it is, why it's mandatory, which hospitals are affected, and how the target price is calculated. No jargon — written for a physician who has never heard of a bundled payment.

→ TEAM Overview

Know what your documentation actually does

How a diagnosis moves from your note to a DRG tier to a payment. Why "heart failure" and "acute systolic heart failure" are not the same code. Why lab values are not diagnoses.

→ CDI Fundamentals

See exactly which conditions to document for your procedure

Ranked MCCs, ranked CCs, phrasing examples, and a discharge checklist — one page per procedure. Print it. Bookmark it. Use it before every discharge.

→ LEJR · SHFFT · Spinal Fusion · CABG · Major Bowel — Quick Reference Cards

Understand the CC/MCC system completely

Every high-value CC and MCC across all five procedures — with the common documentation miss for each and the clinical criteria that must be present to justify the diagnosis.

→ CC/MCC Reference

Understand HCCs and the target price

What HCCs are, how they differ from CCs and MCCs, and which chronic conditions in your patient population — if accurately documented in the six months before surgery — raise the episode's target price.

→ HCC Reference — General · LEJR · SHFFT · Spinal Fusion · CABG · Major Bowel

Know what happens after discharge

How discharge disposition, SNF selection, DME orders, and readmission prevention connect to episode cost — and which of those decisions are yours to make.

→ Your Orders, Your Episode

Understand the full quality picture

How APR-DRG severity scoring affects your hospital's quality rankings, commercial contracts, and Medicaid payment — and why it runs in parallel with the MS-DRG system you already know.

→ APR-DRG SOI/ROM Reference

One More Thing

This playbook is not about upcoding. It is not about adding diagnoses that are not clinically supported. Every phrasing example, every checklist item, every "write this instead of that" assumes the condition is present and being treated.

The problem CDI programs exist to solve is not fraud — it is the gap between what clinicians know and what the medical record says. A patient with AKI who is getting IV fluids and nephrology consults has AKI. A discharge summary that says "creatinine elevated, monitoring" does not say AKI. The condition is real. The documentation does not reflect it. That is the gap.

Closing that gap is accurate medicine and accurate documentation. It is also what makes the payment system work the way it was designed to.

TEAM Playbook · For physicians and APPs at TEAM-participating hospitals

Content reflects CMS TEAM model as finalized in FY2025/FY2026 IPPS Final Rules
