/learn/team-overview.title: What Is TEAM?
/learn/team-overview.html:
What Is TEAM?

Starting January 1, 2026, CMS changed how Medicare pays for five common surgical procedures at hundreds of hospitals across the country. If your hospital is in a selected region, you are participating whether you opted in or not. This module explains what changed, what it means for your patients, and why your documentation is one of the most direct levers you have.

TEAM Pearl

TEAM is mandatory. It is not a voluntary pilot. There is no opt-out for hospitals in selected geographic areas. Every Medicare fee-for-service patient you operate on in one of the five covered procedures is part of a TEAM episode — automatically, starting with your first case in 2026.

The Core Idea in Plain Language

Before TEAM, Medicare paid for each service separately: the surgery, the hospitalization, the SNF stay, the home health visits, the readmission — each as its own transaction. Hospitals and physicians were paid regardless of how efficiently or effectively the episode unfolded overall.

TEAM bundles all of that into a single episode. Each episode includes the anchor hospitalization and a 30-day post-acute period, starting on the first day of discharge for inpatient procedures or the day of the procedure for outpatient cases. Medicare adds up every non-excluded claim during that window — inpatient, outpatient, SNF, home health, rehab, readmissions, physician fees, labs, DME — and compares the total to a pre-set target price.

If actual costs are below the target and quality standards are met, the hospital may receive a reconciliation payment. If costs exceed the target, the hospital may owe CMS money, unless they are in a non-risk or limited-risk track.

That is the model. Spend less than the target, with good quality: you benefit. Spend more: you owe. Your documentation affects both sides of that equation.

Which Hospitals Are Affected

Acute care hospitals paid under IPPS and OPPS located in selected Core-Based Statistical Areas (CBSAs) across the U.S. are required to participate. Selected CBSAs were published in the FY 2025 IPPS final rule and capture a mix of hospitals with different value-based care experiences.

Hospitals that participated through the end of BPCI Advanced or CJR were eligible to voluntarily opt in; everyone else in a selected CBSA is mandatory. If you are unsure whether your hospital is in a selected region, your hospital administration will know — this is not something a physician needs to determine independently.

Note

TEAM covers only Original Medicare (Part A and B) beneficiaries. Patients with Medicare Advantage, managed Medicare, or Medicare eligibility due to end-stage renal disease are excluded from TEAM episodes. Not every patient you operate on is in a TEAM episode — but for those who are, you will not know at the time of surgery.

The Five Procedures

Episodes of focus are Lower Extremity Joint Replacement, Surgical Hip Femur Fracture Treatment, Spinal Fusion, Coronary Artery Bypass Graft, and Major Bowel Procedure.

In brief:

Lower Extremity Joint Replacement (LEJR) — total hip, total knee, and total ankle arthroplasty. Both elective cases and urgent fracture cases are included. Triggered by MS-DRG 469, 470, 521, 522, or outpatient CPT codes 27130, 27447, 27702.

Surgical Hip/Femur Fracture Treatment (SHFFT) — operative treatment of hip and femur fractures in Medicare patients. Often a higher-risk, less elective population than LEJR.

Spinal Fusion — a wide family of procedures across cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions, both anterior and posterior approaches. DRG family varies by level and complexity.

Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG) — on-pump and off-pump CABG, including cases with concomitant valve or other cardiac procedures. DRG family determined by concomitant procedure.

Major Bowel Procedure — resections, ostomies, and related operations across colorectal, small bowel, and related structures. Includes both elective and emergency presentations.

The Target Price: What It Is and How It's Set

The target price is the number your hospital's episode spending will be measured against. Understanding how it is built clarifies why documentation matters.

TEAM target prices are based on Medicare FFS episode spending across all hospitals in the hospital's geographic region during the baseline period, not the individual hospital's own spending history. Every participating hospital in a region starts from the same benchmark, regardless of its historical spending levels.

For each performance year, CMS establishes a three-year baseline period of historical clinical episodes. The baseline period rolls forward each year so that the most recent data is incorporated. For Performance Year 1 (calendar year 2026), the baseline is 2022–2024.

The formula for the hospital-specific target price adds several adjustments on top of that regional benchmark:

Prospective trend factor — adjusts for expected changes in spending between the baseline period and the performance year.

Risk adjustment multiplier — the critical one for documentation purposes. Risk adjustment at the beneficiary level includes age (four brackets), beneficiary economic risk using the Community Deprivation Index, and HCC count risk adjustment factor — for beneficiaries with 0, 1, 2, 3, or 4+ HCCs — found on a 180-day lookback ending one day prior to episode initiation.

Discount factor — represents Medicare's portion of savings: 1.5% for CABG and major bowel procedures, and 2% for LEJR, SHFFT, and spinal fusion. This is CMS's built-in margin — the target price is already set slightly below the expected spend to generate savings for the program.

The documentation implication: HCCs documented in the 180 days before surgery directly raise your patient's risk adjustment multiplier, which raises your target price, which gives you more room to operate within the bundle. A patient with four documented HCCs generates a higher target price than the same patient with no documented HCCs. If that patient's comorbidities are real but undocumented, the hospital absorbs the difference.

Note

The risk adjustment lookback is 180 days prior to episode initiation. HCC documentation from ambulatory visits, pre-admission testing, and any inpatient encounter in the six months before surgery all count — not just the operative hospitalization itself.

Quality Measures and Reconciliation

Hitting the target price is not enough on its own. Performance on quality measures can modify reconciliation payments by up to ±10%, making quality performance essential.

Three quality measures influence the final reconciliation amount: the Hybrid Hospital-Wide All-Cause Readmission Measure with Claims and EHR Data, the CMS Patient Safety and Adverse Events Composite, and — for LEJR — the Hospital-Level Total Hip and/or Total Knee Arthroplasty Patient Reported Outcome-Based Performance Measure (PRO-PM).

These measures are risk-adjusted using the same coded diagnosis data that drives DRG assignment. A hospital with a poorly documented patient population will appear to have worse risk-adjusted readmission and complication rates than their clinical performance actually warrants — because the benchmark for "expected" outcomes was built on an underdocumented comorbidity profile.

This is the second place documentation affects TEAM performance: not just the target price, but the quality benchmark against which outcomes are measured.

Participation Tracks

TEAM has graduated risk through different participation tracks to accommodate different levels of risk and reward and allow participants to ease into full-risk participation.

TrackWhoFinancial Risk
Track 1All hospitals, PY1; safety-net hospitals, PY1–3Upside only — up to 10% bonus, no penalty
Track 2Safety-net, rural, Medicare-dependent, sole community, PY2–5±5% cap
Track 3All hospitals, all years±20% cap

In practical terms: in 2026 (Performance Year 1), no hospital owes CMS money. Every participating hospital is in Track 1 with upside-only risk. Starting in Performance Year 2, most hospitals move to Track 3 unless they qualify for Track 2 protection. Track 3's 20% stop-loss represents meaningful financial exposure at volume.

Note

Reconciliation occurs six months after each performance year ends, to allow for late claims. The financial consequence of a full year's episodes lands as a single payment or repayment roughly 18 months after the first case. This lag means the data and documentation decisions made today won't show up as a check or a bill until well into the following year.

How TEAM Differs From BPCI and CJR

Many surgeons — particularly in orthopedics and cardiac surgery — have prior experience with bundled payment models. TEAM shares their structure but differs in important ways.

BPCI (Bundled Payments for Care Improvement, 2013–2018) and BPCI Advanced (2018–2025) were voluntary. Hospitals and physician groups opted in, selected which episode types to include, and could exit the program. BPCI had limited enforcement of care coordination standards. Participants with efficient practice patterns selected themselves in; others stayed out.

CJR (Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement, 2016–2025) was mandatory for hip and knee replacement in selected MSAs and demonstrated that bundled payments could reduce costs without compromising outcomes in high-volume orthopedic procedures. CJR included post-acute care services for 90 days after discharge — a longer window than TEAM's 30 days.

TEAM is mandatory, covers five procedure families instead of one, uses a 30-day post-acute window, and incorporates HCC-based risk adjustment that directly links pre-episode documentation to the financial benchmark. The mandatory, multi-specialty scope means the program captures hospitals and surgeons who have never participated in value-based care before.

Note

While orthopaedic surgeons' Part B payments represent only 12% of total LEJR reimbursement, surgeons control approximately 90% of the cost of care through clinical decision-making and orders. The same principle applies across the other four procedure families. The physician is the clinical decision-maker; the hospital carries the financial accountability. That relationship requires active collaboration — not passive coexistence.

What This Means for Your Practice

TEAM does not change how you are individually paid. Your Part B fee-for-service payments continue as before. The model creates financial accountability at the hospital level, not the individual physician level.

What it changes is the context around your practice:

Your documentation affects the target price. HCCs documented in the 180 days before surgery raise the risk-adjusted benchmark. Underdocumented comorbidities lower it, making the episode look more expensive than it should. This is not a billing issue — it is a data accuracy issue that directly affects whether your hospital's episode performance looks good or bad.

Your discharge documentation affects quality metrics. Risk-adjusted readmission and complication rates depend on coded comorbidity data. If a patient readmits with a complication that was foreseeable given their clinical complexity, that readmission looks worse when the complexity wasn't documented.

Your post-discharge decisions drive episode cost. Discharge disposition — home, home with PT, SNF, inpatient rehab — is the largest variable cost in most episodes after the anchor hospitalization. Reducing unnecessary SNF placement, shortening SNF stays when appropriate, and ensuring patients transition to home with appropriate support are the primary levers most institutions pull.

Your participation in care coordination matters. Surgeon-led, multidisciplinary care has demonstrated the greatest level of improvement in overall patient outcomes, including decreases in length of stay, increased proportion of discharge to home, reduction in 90-day readmission rates and reduction in complication rates. Clinical leadership — not just clinical execution — is what moves the needle.

TEAM Pearl

TEAM does not ask you to do less. It asks you to document what you already know, coordinate care you already believe in, and make discharge decisions you would make anyway for a well-informed patient. The model creates financial consequences for systemic failures that were previously invisible. Your documentation is how the system knows how sick your patients actually were.

The Documentation Connection

The rest of this playbook goes deep on documentation mechanics. Here is the summary at the TEAM level:

Before surgery (180-day HCC window): Chronic conditions documented at any outpatient visit or pre-admission encounter contribute to the risk adjustment multiplier. Diabetes with complications, heart failure, COPD, CKD, dementia, morbid obesity, and many others raise the target price when accurately documented. The same conditions unrecorded lower it.

During the hospitalization (DRG tier): Secondary diagnoses — MCCs and CCs — determine the MS-DRG tier, which drives the hospital's per-episode payment for the anchor stay. The DRG itself is part of the episode cost calculation. A higher-tier DRG reflects a more complex patient and is the accurate code for that patient.

At discharge (quality benchmarking): The discharge summary is the last opportunity to ensure the full clinical picture is coded. Risk-adjusted quality measures use that coded data to set expected outcomes. An incomplete discharge summary produces a distorted quality benchmark.

None of this requires documenting things that aren't present. It requires documenting what is present with enough specificity that the coding system can represent it accurately. That is the goal of everything that follows in this playbook.

/learn/surgical-decisions-and-cost.title: Your Orders, Your Episode: How Surgical Decisions Drive TEAM Cost
/learn/surgical-decisions-and-cost.html:
Your Orders, Your Episode: How Surgical Decisions Drive TEAM Cost

Under TEAM, every Medicare claim for 30 days after your patient's discharge counts against a single target price. The anchor hospitalization is largely fixed once the patient is on the table. What happens after that — where they go, what equipment they receive, whether they come back — is determined almost entirely by decisions your team makes. Not case management. Not the hospitalist. Not administration. Your team.

This module maps five specific clinical decisions to their dollar consequences under TEAM. Each one is yours to make. Each one has a measurable cost range. Taken together, they represent the difference between an episode that performs and one that doesn't.

TEAM Pearl

Surgeons control approximately 90% of the cost of care through clinical decision-making and orders, while receiving roughly 12% of the total episode payment. That leverage cuts both ways: it is the reason surgical leadership in TEAM programs matters, and the reason your documentation and discharge decisions have consequences that extend well beyond your fee.

The Cost Context: What's at Stake by Procedure

Before the five decisions, a frame. Post-acute costs are not evenly distributed across TEAM procedures, which means the decisions below carry different weights depending on what you operate on.

ProcedurePost-acute share of total episodeReadmission cost (avg)
SHFFT (hip fracture)~38–54%~$15,100
LEJR (joint replacement)~21–27%~$15,100
Major Bowel~21%~$15,100
Spinal Fusion~18%~$15,100
CABG~14%~$15,100

For SHFFT, more than half the episode cost happens after you close. For CABG, post-acute is a smaller share — but readmission is just as expensive and more frequent. The decisions below apply across all five procedures; the relative weight of each shifts by procedure type.

Decision 1: Where Does This Patient Go After Discharge?

The decision: Home with home health, outpatient PT, SNF, or IRF.

Why it's yours: The discharge disposition order originates with the surgical or attending team. Case management executes it. The physician's clinical judgment — documented in the discharge summary — is the rationale that determines, defends, and directs where the patient goes.

What it costs:

Discharge destinationTypical Medicare cost to episode
Home with outpatient PT~$800–$2,000
Home with home health~$2,000–$4,000
Skilled Nursing Facility (14 days)~$7,000–$12,000
Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility (10–14 days)~$18,000–$25,000

Every dollar in this table comes out of the same pool that determines whether your hospital earns a reconciliation payment or owes one. A patient discharged to home with home health costs the episode roughly $20,000 less than a patient admitted to IRF. That differential is not a billing curiosity — it is direct episode exposure.

Home health is the clear winner in bundled joint care. It costs less, patients tend to prefer it, and early-discharge-to-home plans cut inpatient days that drive up episode costs. For most elective joint replacement patients with adequate home support, home health with physical therapy is clinically equivalent to SNF at a fraction of the cost. Both BPCI program participants who achieved the most savings — reducing episode costs by 17–18% — did so almost entirely in the post-discharge phase, by decreasing discharges to institutional post-acute care and reducing SNF length of stay.

What justifies SNF: A patient who cannot safely manage at home — due to functional limitations, fall risk, inadequate home support, or wound care complexity — genuinely needs SNF-level care. Document that clinical rationale explicitly. "Patient unable to ambulate independently, lives alone without caregiver support, requires daily wound care — SNF placement medically necessary" is defensible and accurate. "SNF per patient preference" or "complex medical history" is not sufficient clinical justification under TEAM scrutiny.

Patient rights and informed choice: Patients have the right to choose their post-acute setting. What changes under TEAM is the obligation to present an informed choice, not a default. A patient told "you'll go to Sunridge Rehab" has not been given a choice. A patient told "most people in your situation go home with a physical therapist coming to the house — here is what that looks like, and here is what a rehab facility would look like" has been given one. Informed patients, given accurate information, choose home at higher rates than patients given no information.

[PHRASING]

❌ "Discharge to SNF — complex medical history, multiple comorbidities." — Comorbidities do not justify SNF. Functional limitations and care needs do.

✅ "Patient ambulating 75 feet with walker on POD2, tolerating PT twice daily, adequate home support confirmed. Discharge to home with home health PT ordered."

Decision 2: Does This Patient Need IRF?

The decision: Whether to certify a patient for inpatient rehabilitation facility admission.

Why it's yours: Medicare requires physician certification that the patient requires intensive rehabilitation (≥3 hours of active therapy per day), continued medical supervision by a physician, and coordinated multidisciplinary care. In most hospitals, the attending surgeon or hospitalist signs this certification. That signature is the gating document for a $18,000–$25,000 Medicare claim.

The clinical standard: IRF is designed for patients recovering from stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury, and severe burns — conditions requiring hospital-level medical management alongside intensive rehabilitation. For these patients, IRF is the right setting and the right cost. For patients who need rehabilitation but not daily physician supervision and not three hours of active therapy, SNF or home health is the appropriate — and far less expensive — setting.

The key distinction is not how sick the patient is. It is whether they need the specific intensity that defines an IRF admission. A patient with obesity, heart failure, and diabetes who had an uncomplicated total knee replacement does not automatically need IRF. Their comorbidities make them complex — but the question for IRF appropriateness is whether they require intensive rehab and daily physician supervision, not whether their problem list is long.

CJR experience showed this clearly: when hospitals had a financial incentive to examine their IRF referral patterns, many referrals that had been reflexive turned out to be SNF-appropriate or home-appropriate. The patients did not suffer. The episodes cost less.

The financial magnitude at scale: In a program doing 200 LEJR cases annually, if 20% of patients are going to IRF when home health is clinically appropriate, that is 40 episodes carrying a $15,000–$20,000 cost differential each — $600,000 to $800,000 in annual episode overspend attributable to a single discharge pattern.

[PHRASING]

❌ "Patient deconditioned and elderly, recommend IRF for intensive rehabilitation." — Deconditioning and age alone do not meet IRF criteria.

✅ "Patient requires intensive inpatient rehabilitation: unable to tolerate >1 hour of PT daily in current condition, requires daily physician management of [specific condition], coordinated multidisciplinary care medically necessary. IRF certified."

Denial Risk

IRF admissions are audited by Medicare. The three-part criteria — intensive therapy, physician supervision, coordinated care — must all be documented in the certification. An IRF admission that is reversed on audit recaptures the full claim value against the episode.

Decision 3: What Does Your Discharge Summary Tell the SNF?

The decision: What you write — or don't write — in the discharge summary for patients going to SNF.

Why it's yours: The admitting SNF team reads your discharge summary. It is the primary clinical handoff. If it tells them when the patient should go home, they manage toward that target. If it doesn't, they default to caution and extended stays.

How this controls SNF length of stay: The most common cause of prolonged SNF stays is ambiguous or absent discharge criteria. SNF staff are cautious professionals managing liability. Without explicit milestones, "when can this patient go home?" has no answer, so they err toward longer stays. CJR was associated with a 0.76-day reduction in average SNF length of stay and nearly $500 less in SNF spending per episode — roughly correlated with hospitals that started writing better discharge criteria as part of bundle management.

A 14-day SNF stay for joint replacement costs Medicare $7,000–$12,000. An 18-day stay costs $3,000–$5,000 more. The difference is often not clinical complexity — it is whether anyone told the SNF what the endpoint looks like.

What to write: Functional discharge criteria should be specific, measurable, and tied to your clinical pathway. Not "when patient is ready" or "when patient meets SNF criteria for discharge." Those phrases mean nothing actionable to the SNF team.

[PHRASING]

❌ "Discharge to SNF for continued recovery and physical therapy. Follow up with surgeon in 2 weeks." — No functional milestones. SNF has no target.

✅ "Discharge to SNF for continued rehabilitation. Goals for transition to home: independent ambulation 100 feet with assistive device, ability to manage one flight of stairs, wound intact without signs of infection, adequate home support confirmed. Expected SNF duration 7–10 days pending PT progression."

Beyond LOS — SNF selection matters too. SNF quality varies significantly in readmission rates, discharge-to-home rates, and LOS by procedure type. A facility that performs well for orthopedic cases may perform poorly for CABG patients. Hospitals that analyzed their referral patterns and built preferred SNF networks — steering patients to higher-performing facilities based on outcomes data — reduced SNF LOS and readmission rates without restricting patient access. This is a case management and administration function, but surgeons who know which local SNFs have strong orthopedic or cardiac rehab programs make better referrals.

Decision 4: What Happens in the First 10 Days After Discharge?

The decision: Whether there is a structured post-discharge contact protocol and early follow-up, and what the escalation pathway is when something goes wrong.

Why it's yours: The surgical team defines the post-discharge care structure. Whether there is a 48-hour nurse phone call, when the first office visit is, and what number the patient calls at 10pm with a wound question — these are clinical program decisions, not administrative ones. The surgical team sets the protocol; others execute it.

The cost of the readmission you prevent: The average readmission in a TEAM episode costs ~$15,100 and lands entirely against the episode target. It also triggers the quality adjustment — the Hybrid Hospital-Wide All-Cause Readmission Measure modifies reconciliation by up to ±10% across all episodes. One readmission is a cost event. A pattern of readmissions is a quality penalty on top of the cost.

Readmission causes differ by procedure, and the timing pattern matters for how you design surveillance:

LEJR: Surgical readmissions (wound infection, joint instability, DVT/PE) occur earlier — mean 18 days post-discharge. Medical readmissions (cardiac, urinary retention, ileus) occur later — mean 33 days. Early contact should screen for wound and surgical issues; later follow-up should screen for medical decompensation.

SHFFT: Medical readmission dominates — cardiac events, pneumonia, UTI, delirium. These patients need post-acute facilities capable of managing medical complexity, not just rehabilitation. The discharge summary should specify the patient's medical management needs alongside rehabilitation goals.

CABG: 30-day readmission rate is approximately 12.9%. Most common causes are infection and sepsis, cardiac arrhythmia, congestive heart failure, respiratory complications, and pleural effusion. Pleural effusion develops predictably after CABG — it is not a surprise complication, and a structured 7–10 day follow-up with imaging is the intervention that catches it before it becomes a readmission. Many CABG readmissions represent conditions that were developing at discharge and were not addressed before the patient left.

Major Bowel: Ileus, bowel obstruction, anastomotic complications, dehydration, and ostomy complications dominate. Ostomy patients have particularly high readmission rates from complications and inadequate self-care. A dedicated ostomy nurse follow-up call at 48–72 hours is among the highest-yield single interventions in this population.

Spinal Fusion: Wound complications, surgical site infection, hardware complications, and VTE. High VTE risk makes anticoagulation management and early mobility protocols relevant.

The highest-yield post-discharge interventions:

A nurse phone call at 48–72 hours is the single most consistently effective readmission prevention intervention across all surgical episode types. The call confirms wound care, medication adherence, and warning signs — and catches confusion about follow-up appointments before it becomes a no-show that delays recognition of a problem.

Early surgical follow-up at 7–10 days — not 2–3 weeks — is the clinical checkpoint that catches complications in the window when they are still manageable. Wound issues caught at day 7 are treated with antibiotics and wound care. The same issues caught at day 21 via readmission are treated with debridement and a $15,000 hospitalization.

A clear escalation pathway — a specific phone number, answered by a nurse who can triage — makes it easier for patients to call than to go to the ED. Most ED visits by surgical patients in the 30-day window become admissions. Most of those admissions were for problems that a triage nurse call could have managed.

TEAM Pearl

The single most important post-discharge decision is structural: make it easier for your patient to call you than to call 911. A patient with a wound question at 9pm who has a direct nurse contact number will call. The same patient with no number will go to the ED. Most of those visits become the $15,100 admission that erases your episode margin.

Decision 5: Should This Patient Have Surgery Now?

The decision: Whether to proceed with elective surgery or delay for optimization.

Why it's yours: No one else can make this call. Anesthesia can refuse, but they cannot reschedule. Case management can flag risk, but they cannot delay the case. The decision to operate, delay, and under what optimization conditions, belongs to the surgeon.

Why it's the highest-leverage decision in the episode: Every downstream cost — SNF, IRF, readmission, DME, post-discharge nursing — is downstream of a patient who was either well-prepared for surgery or wasn't. An A1c of 11 at the time of elective knee replacement predicts wound infection, slow healing, and extended recovery. Uncontrolled heart failure predicts prolonged hospital stay, SNF placement, and readmission. Active UTI before joint replacement predicts prosthetic joint infection — a catastrophic complication that costs tens of thousands of dollars and destroys the patient's outcome.

Under fee-for-service, there was no financial consequence at the episode level for proceeding with a poorly optimized patient. Under TEAM, the downstream costs of that decision accumulate in a single episode account. The incentive to optimize is now financial as well as clinical.

Optimization thresholds worth standardizing for elective procedures:

VariableThreshold to consider delay
HbA1c>8.0 (consider; >9.0 strong reason to delay)
BMI>40 — assess functional mobility and home support
Active infectionAny active site infection — delay until resolved
Decompensated heart failureDelay until euvolemic and stable
Uncontrolled hypertension>180/110 persistent — optimize before proceeding
Nutritional statusAlbumin <3.0 or severe malnutrition — nutrition consult, consider delay
Social supportNo caregiver at home for high-complexity patients — confirm support plan before scheduling
Note

Optimization thresholds should be established as a program-level policy, not applied inconsistently by individual surgeon preference. A shared protocol gives the surgical team clinical cover to delay cases, gives patients clear expectations, and produces outcomes data that demonstrates the program's commitment to appropriate patient selection.

The TEAM financial logic: A patient with an A1c of 11 who develops a wound infection and readmits generates approximately $15,100 in readmission costs plus extended home health and additional DME. A one-to-two month delay for glycemic optimization costs the patient nothing clinical and costs the episode nothing. The math strongly favors the delay.

[PHRASING]

❌ "Patient eager to proceed, will optimize postoperatively." — Postoperative optimization does not reduce perioperative and episode risk.

✅ "Elective LEJR deferred pending glycemic optimization. A1c currently 10.2. Target A1c <8.0 before proceeding. Patient referred to PCP for diabetes management. Reschedule in 6–8 weeks pending lab results."

A Note on DME Orders

DME is not a major cost driver relative to the decisions above, but it deserves mention because it is entirely order-driven. Under TEAM, all Part B DME claims in the 30-day episode window count against the target.

Walker, raised toilet seat, shower chair, and cane are appropriate and expected. The discipline is on the edges: wound VAC duration should be actively managed and discontinued when healing is confirmed; CPM devices for TKA have limited evidence for routine use and should be ordered when specifically indicated; TENS and nerve stimulator units should be documented for medical necessity if ordered. A wound VAC running 45 days beyond clinical need is not a large cost item individually — but at program volume, reflexive and indefinite DME orders are a consistent minor drag that clinical discipline can eliminate.

Quick Reference: Five Decisions and Their Episode Cost

DecisionLow-cost outcomeHigh-cost outcomeCost differential
Discharge destinationHome + home health (~$2,000–$4,000)IRF (~$18,000–$25,000)Up to ~$22,000 per episode
IRF certificationNot certified (appropriate)Certified when SNF/home sufficient$15,000–$20,000 per episode
Discharge summary qualitySpecific milestones → 7–10 day SNF stayVague → 14–21 day SNF stay$3,000–$8,000 per episode
Post-discharge follow-up48-hr call + 7-day visit → prevented readmissionNo contact → avoidable readmission~$15,100 per readmission
Pre-op optimizationOptimized patient, clean episodeUnoptimized → wound infection, readmission$15,000–$30,000+ per complication

Readmission causes by procedure — what to screen for:

ProcedureEarly window (days 1–21)Late window (days 22–30)
LEJRWound infection, DVT/PE, joint complicationMedical decompensation, cardiac, urinary
SHFFTDelirium, fall, medical complicationPneumonia, UTI, cardiac
CABGArrhythmia, pleural effusion, wound infectionCHF, respiratory, sepsis

/reference/major-bowel.html:
TEAM Quick Reference — Major Bowel Procedure

DRGs: 329 (with MCC) · 330 (with CC) · 331 (without CC/MCC)

Tier structure: 3-tier — both MCCs and CCs move payment. This is the widest payment spread of all five TEAM procedures.

~Payment delta MCC → CC: ~$8,000–$12,000 · CC → base: ~$4,000–$6,000 (national averages; vary by wage index)

Patient population note: Includes elective resections (cancer, diverticular disease, IBD) and emergent cases (obstruction, perforation, ischemia). Comorbidity profiles differ significantly — emergency patients have no pre-op encounter for HCC capture.

Top 5 MCCs — Highest Payment Impact

#MCCWhy It's MissedICD-10
1Sepsis / Severe Sepsis / Septic Shock"Infection" or "peritonitis" documented without linking to systemic sepsis; source not namedA41.x + R65.20/R65.21
2Acute Kidney InjuryCreatinine elevation in septic or hypovolemic patient documented as lab value, not AKI diagnosisN17.0–N17.9
3Severe Protein-Calorie MalnutritionDietitian documents it; physician never does — only physician diagnosis is codeableE43
4Metastatic Disease"History of cancer" written for patients with active metastatic disease under treatment — active disease requires active disease codingC77.x–C79.x
5Acute Respiratory Failure"Prolonged intubation" or "ventilator dependent" without naming respiratory failureJ96.01, J96.02

Also consider: Metabolic/toxic encephalopathy (G93.41), intestinal perforation when principal dx supports it (K63.1), acute systolic/diastolic HF (I50.21–I50.43), acute pancreatitis (K85.x)

Top 10 CCs — Payment and Quality Value

Clinical Note

In Major Bowel's 3-tier structure, CCs directly increase DRG payment. Document all that apply.

#CCCommon MissICD-10
1Moderate malnutritionNo physician diagnosis despite dietitian assessment, weight loss, or poor intakeE44.0
2Acute blood loss anemia"Postop anemia" without type; transfusion ordered without named diagnosisD62
3Ileus (postoperative)"Slow GI recovery" or "not tolerating diet" instead of ileus diagnosisK56.7
4Chronic systolic or diastolic HF (stable)"CHF" unspecified — no CC/MCC capturedI50.22, I50.32
5COPD with acute exacerbation"COPD" without exacerbation; "breathing problems"J44.1
6Diabetes with complications"Diabetes" alone without specifying complication typeE11.40–E11.69
7Atrial fibrillation (specified type)"A-fib" without type; undocumented entirelyI48.0, I48.11, I48.19
8Peritonitis (when not principal dx)Present in perforation cases; may need explicit documentation as secondary dxK65.0–K65.9
9C. difficile enteritisPositive C. diff during hospitalization; diagnosis not namedA04.71, A04.72
10Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40)"Obese" or "BMI 42" written without diagnosis — Z68 code alone is not a CCE66.01

Key HCCs — Target Price Risk Adjustment

Major Bowel has 13 HCC risk adjustment variables, with the most oncology-specific HCC categories of any TEAM procedure.

HCCConditionDocumentation Trigger
8/17Metastatic cancerActive metastatic disease — not "history of cancer." Specify current sites and treatment intent
11Colorectal / bladder cancer (active)Stage, current treatment status — "history of colon cancer" ≠ active cancer under treatment
9/10/12Other active malignancyLung, head/neck, brain, breast, prostate — specify stage and whether under active treatment
85Congestive heart failureSpecify systolic vs. diastolic; acute vs. chronic
37Diabetes with chronic complicationsName the complication; avoid "DM" alone
48Morbid obesityBMI ≥40 or BMI 35-39.9 with comorbidities + provider diagnosis (E66.01, HCC 48)
280COPDSeverity and exacerbation status
54Drug/alcohol dependenceActive substance use disorder — not "history of" if currently active

Emergency case note: No pre-op encounter exists for emergent bowel cases. The ED assessment and admission H&P are the only HCC capture documents. Treat them accordingly — name every active comorbidity explicitly.

Exact Phrasing Examples

Sepsis (highest-yield MCC for major bowel)

Instead of: "Patient with peritonitis from perforated diverticulitis — started on broad-spectrum antibiotics."

Write: "Sepsis (A41.89) due to perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with feculent peritonitis (K57.20). Meeting Sepsis-3 criteria — SOFA score increased ≥2 from baseline with hypotension and elevated lactate. IV antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors initiated."

Active cancer vs. history (most critical HCC distinction for major bowel)

Instead of: "History of colon cancer, s/p hemicolectomy, currently on chemotherapy."

Write: "Stage III colon cancer (C18.7), post right hemicolectomy 8 months ago, currently on adjuvant FOLFOX cycle 6 of 12. Active malignancy under treatment — not in remission."

Instead of: "Metastatic colon cancer — palliative intent."

Write: "Metastatic colorectal cancer (C18.7) with hepatic metastases (C78.7) and peritoneal carcinomatosis (C78.6). Palliative systemic therapy with FOLFIRI ongoing. No curative intent."

Morbid Obesity

Instead of: "Obese, BMI 37.5, history of sleep apnea."

Write: "Morbid obesity due to comorbidities (BMI 37.5, obstructive sleep apnea) — patient's severe obesity requires bariatric bed, custom mobilization protocol, and active CPAP compliance monitoring postoperatively."

Malnutrition

Instead of: "Patient with poor nutritional status, dietitian following."

Write: "Severe protein-calorie malnutrition (E43) — >10% unintentional weight loss over 2 months in setting of active malignancy, significant muscle and fat wasting, albumin 2.0. ASPEN criteria for severe malnutrition met. TPN initiated."

AKI in septic patient

Instead of: "Creatinine up in setting of sepsis — IV fluids running."

Write: "Acute kidney injury stage 3 (N17.9), in the setting of septic shock — creatinine peaked at 4.1 from baseline 0.9. Continuous renal replacement therapy initiated. Nephrology co-managing."

Ileus

Instead of: "Slow GI recovery — NPO, NG tube in place."

Write: "Postoperative ileus (K56.7) — absent bowel sounds, abdominal distension, NG tube output >800mL/day. NPO, NG tube decompression, ambulation protocol initiated."

Ostomy complication (discharge-specific)

Instead of: "Ostomy functioning, teaching provided."

Write: "High-output ileostomy with dehydration risk — output averaging 1,800mL/day. Electrolyte replacement protocol initiated, ostomy nurse education provided, explicit written instructions for hydration and dietary management given to patient and family. Follow-up with ostomy nurse at 48 hours post-discharge arranged."

Discharge Documentation Checklist

Before signing the discharge summary, confirm:

  • [ ] Sepsis — if systemic infection with organ dysfunction: document sepsis with source explicitly; do not leave as "peritonitis" or "infection" alone
  • [ ] Cancer status — if patient has active malignancy under treatment: document as active cancer with stage and treatment, not "history of cancer"
  • [ ] Metastatic disease — document current metastatic sites and treatment intent (curative vs. palliative)
  • [ ] AKI — if creatinine rose at any point: document AKI with stage and etiology; especially important in septic/hypovolemic patients
  • [ ] Malnutrition — if weight loss, wasting, low albumin, or TPN/enteral nutrition initiated: physician documents severity (mild/moderate/severe)
  • [ ] Respiratory failure — if ventilator weaning prolonged or re-intubation required: document acute respiratory failure explicitly
  • [ ] Ileus — if NG tube placed, NPO prolonged, or GI decompression required: document postoperative ileus as diagnosis
  • [ ] Ostomy — if ostomy created: document type and output status; specify complications if present; document discharge education plan
  • [ ] Anemia — if transfusion given: document acute blood loss anemia (D62)
  • [ ] Hyponatremia / electrolyte disorders — if Na <135 or other electrolyte abnormality required management: document as diagnosis
  • [ ] Diabetes — specify type and complications; insulin management during hospitalization implies relevant complexity
  • [ ] C. difficile — if C. diff positive during stay: document as diagnosis, not just "positive culture"
  • [ ] Heart failure — if diuresis or volume management required: specify systolic vs. diastolic, acute vs. chronic
  • [ ] COPD — if respiratory involvement during stay: document exacerbation status
  • [ ] Morbid Obesity — if BMI is ≥40, or BMI is 35–39.9 with severe weight-exacerbated comorbidities: document "morbid obesity" to capture CC (+0.7127 weight shift on DRG 330) and HCC 48
  • [ ] POA status — all secondary diagnoses should reflect whether present on admission; critical for perforation, peritonitis cases where POA timing matters

Source: CMS MS-DRG V43.0 · FY2026 ICD-10-CM · Last updated June 2026

Payment figures are national averages; vary by hospital wage index. CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule.

#MCCWhy It's MissedICD-10
1Acute Systolic or Diastolic Heart Failure"CHF" documented instead — not an MCC; unspecified heart failure has no CC/MCC valueI50.21, I50.23, I50.31, I50.33
2Acute Kidney InjuryPost-pump AKI described as "creatinine elevation" or "contrast nephropathy" — lab findings, not diagnosisN17.0–N17.9
3Metabolic or Toxic EncephalopathyPost-pump confusion documented as "ICU delirium" or "altered mental status" — delirium is CC, encephalopathy is MCCG93.41, G92.9
4Acute Respiratory Failure"Prolonged intubation" or "ventilator weaning difficulty" without naming respiratory failureJ96.01, J96.02
5Dilated CardiomyopathyUnderlying cardiomyopathy not documented separately from HF — both should be codedI42.0

Also consider: Pulmonary hypertension (I27.0–I27.29), perioperative MI (I97.190–I97.191), sepsis (A41.x + R65.20/R65.21), severe malnutrition (E43)

Top 10 CCs — SOI/ROM and Quality Value

Clinical Note

CCs do not move the CABG DRG payment tier. Document for SOI scoring, risk-adjusted quality metrics, and audit defense.

#CCCommon MissICD-10
1New-onset postop atrial fibrillation"A-fib" without specifying type; "irregular rhythm"; undocumented entirelyI48.0 (paroxysmal), I48.19 (persistent)
2Chronic systolic or diastolic HF (stable)"CHF" unspecified — no CC/MCC at allI50.22, I50.32
3Pleural effusionPresent on many post-CABG patients; rarely named as a diagnosisJ90
4Acute blood loss anemia"Postop anemia" without type; transfusion ordered without diagnosisD62
5Moderate malnutritionNo physician diagnosis despite nutrition support initiatedE44.0
6Demand ischemia (without MI)"Troponin bump" or "demand ischemia" documented vaguely — this is a codeable diagnosisI24.8
7COPD with acute exacerbation"COPD" without exacerbation; "pulmonary disease"J44.1
8Diabetes with complications"Diabetes" or "DM" without specifying complication typeE11.40–E11.69
9Cardiomyopathy (non-ischemic, stable)Underlying cardiomyopathy undocumented when HF is presentI42.0–I42.9
10Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40)"Obese" or "BMI 42" written without diagnosis — Z68 code alone is not a CCE66.01

Key HCCs — Target Price Risk Adjustment

CABG has 12 HCC risk adjustment variables — the fewest of the five procedures. The cardiac surgical population is already identified as high-complexity; the HCC window captures pre-existing comorbidities that predict episode cost.

HCCConditionDocumentation Trigger
85Congestive heart failure (any type)Specify systolic vs. diastolic; include EF if available; avoid "CHF" alone
86Acute MISpecify STEMI vs. NSTEMI; territory if known; this is often the operative indication
87Unstable angina / acute ischemic HDDocument ACS presentation that led to surgery
96Specified arrhythmiasAF type; pre-existing VT — specify at pre-op encounter
107/108Vascular diseasePAD with site and severity; aortic disease
37Diabetes with chronic complicationsName the complication — nephropathy interacts with AKI risk
280COPDSeverity and exacerbation status
327CKD Stage 4Stage the CKD — matters significantly for AKI prediction and management
48Morbid obesityBMI ≥40 or BMI 35-39.9 with weight-exacerbated comorbidities + provider diagnosis

Pre-op cardiology note is the primary HCC source. "Systolic dysfunction" does not code to the same HCC as "chronic systolic heart failure." Cardiologists should use diagnosis language, not functional descriptions.

Exact Phrasing Examples

Heart failure (most important CABG documentation target)

Instead of: "CHF — EF 30%, continue home meds."

Write: "Ischemic cardiomyopathy (I25.5) with chronic systolic heart failure (I50.22), EF 30%, NYHA Class III. Managed with carvedilol, lisinopril, furosemide, and spironolactone."

Post-op atrial fibrillation

Instead of: "Post-op a-fib, rate controlled."

Write: "New-onset paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (I48.0) on POD2, converted to sinus rhythm with amiodarone. Will continue amiodarone 200mg daily for 4 weeks post-discharge."

Clinical Note

If AF is still present at discharge: "Persistent atrial fibrillation (I48.19) — present at discharge, rate controlled on metoprolol and anticoagulated with apixaban."

AKI after bypass

Instead of: "Creatinine rose to 2.1 post-pump, improving. Likely contrast and hypoperfusion."

Write: "Acute kidney injury, stage 2 (N17.9), post-cardiopulmonary bypass, likely ischemic etiology with contribution from contrast exposure. Creatinine peaked at 2.1 from baseline 1.0. IV hydration and nephrotoxin avoidance initiated, nephrology consulted, creatinine trending down."

Perioperative MI

Instead of: "Troponin elevated postop — expected after bypass."

Write: "Perioperative myocardial infarction (I97.190) — troponin I peak 42 ng/mL, new ST changes in inferior leads on POD1, confirmed on repeat ECG. Cardiology co-managing."

Morbid Obesity

Instead of: "Obese, BMI 41.3."

Write: "Morbid obesity (BMI 41.3) — patient's severe obesity requires specialized postoperative mobilization, bariatric bed, and respiratory care monitoring to prevent sternal dehiscence."

Encephalopathy

Instead of: "ICU delirium — reorientation protocol."

Write: "Metabolic encephalopathy (G93.41) secondary to hypoxia and metabolic derangement post-bypass. CAM positive POD1-2. Treating underlying cause; delirium precautions in place."

Dilated cardiomyopathy

Instead of: "Cardiomegaly on CXR, known poor EF."

Write: "Dilated cardiomyopathy (I42.0) — EF 25% on pre-op TTE, left ventricular dilation. Distinct from ischemic cardiomyopathy; non-ischemic etiology confirmed on prior workup."

Discharge Documentation Checklist

Before signing the discharge summary, confirm:

  • [ ] Heart failure — specify systolic vs. diastolic, acute vs. chronic, EF if available; avoid "CHF" alone
  • [ ] Cardiomyopathy — if EF reduced and cardiomyopathy is the underlying diagnosis: document separately from HF (both are codeable)
  • [ ] Postop atrial fibrillation — if AF occurred: document type (paroxysmal if terminated before discharge; persistent if ongoing); document management and discharge plan
  • [ ] AKI — if creatinine rose at any point post-bypass: document AKI with stage and etiology; do not leave as "creatinine elevation"
  • [ ] Encephalopathy — if confusion occurred: distinguish metabolic encephalopathy (MCC) from delirium (CC); document etiology
  • [ ] Perioperative MI — if troponin significantly elevated with ECG changes: document as perioperative MI, not "expected troponin release"
  • [ ] Pleural effusion — present in most CABG patients by discharge: document if clinically relevant and managed
  • [ ] Respiratory failure — if ventilator weaning was prolonged or patient required re-intubation: document acute respiratory failure
  • [ ] Pulmonary hypertension — if documented on pre-op or intra-op right heart cath: document as active diagnosis
  • [ ] Malnutrition — if nutrition support initiated or prolonged ICU course: physician documents severity
  • [ ] Diabetes — specify type and complications; avoid "DM" alone
  • [ ] COPD — if respiratory involvement during stay: document exacerbation status
  • [ ] Morbid Obesity — if BMI is ≥40, or BMI is 35–39.9 with severe weight-exacerbated comorbidities: document "morbid obesity" to capture CC and trigger HCC 48 risk adjustment
  • [ ] POA status — all secondary diagnoses should reflect whether present on admission or developed during stay

Source: CMS MS-DRG V43.0 · FY2026 ICD-10-CM · Last updated June 2026

Payment figures are national averages; vary by hospital wage index. CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule.

/reference/lejr.title: TEAM Quick Reference — Lower Extremity Joint Replacement (LEJR)
/reference/lejr.html:
TEAM Quick Reference — Lower Extremity Joint Replacement

DRGs: 469 (with MCC) · 470 (without CC/MCC) · 521 (hip fracture, with MCC) · 522 (hip fracture, without MCC)

Tier structure: 2-tier — only MCCs move payment. CCs have no DRG payment impact in LEJR. Document CCs for SOI/ROM quality metrics only.

~Payment delta MCC → base: ~$4,500–$6,000 per case (national average; varies by wage index)

Top 5 MCCs — Highest Payment Impact

#MCCWhy It's MissedICD-10
1Acute Kidney Injury (any stage)Creatinine rises documented as lab values, not diagnosesN17.0–N17.9
2Acute Systolic or Diastolic Heart Failure"CHF" or "heart failure" written instead — neither is an MCCI50.21, I50.23, I50.31, I50.33
3Metabolic or Toxic Encephalopathy"Confusion" or "AMS" documented — neither is codeable as encephalopathyG93.41, G92.9
4Severe Protein-Calorie MalnutritionDietitian documents it; physician never does — coder cannot use dietitian-only diagnosisE43
5Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome"Morbid obesity" or "OSA" written instead of OHS — different conditions, different codesE66.2

Also consider: Acute respiratory failure (J96.01), sepsis (A41.x + R65.20/R65.21), acute pulmonary edema (J81.0), acute MI (I21.x)

Top 10 CCs — SOI/ROM and Quality Value

Clinical Note

CCs do not change the LEJR DRG payment tier. Document them for severity-of-illness (SOI) scoring, risk-adjusted quality metrics, and accurate clinical record.

#CCCommon MissICD-10
1Chronic systolic or diastolic HF (stable)"CHF" or "heart failure" (unspecified = no CC/MCC)I50.22, I50.32
2Acute blood loss anemia"Postop anemia" without specifying typeD62
3Atrial fibrillation (any specified type)"A-fib" without type; "irregular rhythm"I48.0, I48.11, I48.19
4COPD with acute exacerbation"COPD" without exacerbationJ44.1
5Obesity hypoventilation syndrome"Morbid obesity" or "OSA on CPAP"E66.2
6Moderate malnutritionNo physician nutrition diagnosis at allE44.0
7Acute DVT"DVT prophylaxis given" — describes treatment, not diagnosisI82.4xx
8CKD Stage IV"CKD" without stagingN18.4
9Drug-induced delirium"Confusion" without etiologyF05
10Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40)"Obese" or "BMI 42" written without diagnosis — Z68 code alone is not a CCE66.01

Key HCCs — Target Price Risk Adjustment

HCCs are documented in the 180 days before surgery and adjust the episode target price — not the DRG. Document these at every pre-op encounter.

HCCConditionDocumentation Trigger
224/225/226Heart failure (any type)Specify systolic vs. diastolic; acute vs. chronic
238Atrial fibrillationSpecify type — paroxysmal, persistent, permanent
280COPDDocument severity and current exacerbation status
37Diabetes with chronic complicationsName the complication — neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy
327CKD Stage 4Stage the CKD explicitly; "CKD" alone is insufficient
48Morbid obesityBMI ≥40 with physician diagnosis; OHS adds E66.2
125/126/127Dementia (any severity)Name it, stage it — "confusion" does not capture the HCC

Annual re-documentation required. "History of CHF" does not count. Must document as active with management plan.

Exact Phrasing Examples

AKI

Instead of: "Creatinine 2.4, slightly elevated, monitoring."

Write: "Acute kidney injury, stage 2 by KDIGO criteria, likely prerenal. Managed with IV fluid resuscitation, nephrology consulted, nephrotoxins held."

Heart failure

Instead of: "CHF — continue home diuretics."

Write: "Acute on chronic systolic heart failure (EF 35%). IV Lasix given with 2L net negative output. Transitioning to oral diuresis."

Encephalopathy

Instead of: "Patient confused postop, likely multifactorial."

Write: "Metabolic encephalopathy secondary to uremia and electrolyte disturbance. CAM positive. Reorientation protocol initiated, underlying metabolic cause being treated."

Malnutrition

Instead of: "Poor appetite, dietary consult placed."

Write: "Moderate protein-calorie malnutrition per ASPEN clinical criteria — significant weight loss, reduced intake, muscle wasting on exam. Nutrition support initiated."

Morbid Obesity

Instead of: "Obese, BMI 42.1."

Write: "Morbid obesity (BMI 42.1) — patient's severe obesity requires specialized post-op mobilization planning and extra personnel for transfer."

OHS

Instead of: "Morbid obesity, on CPAP at home."

Write: "Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (BMI 44, home BiPAP, baseline pCO₂ elevated). CPAP/BiPAP continued in-house."

Discharge Documentation Checklist

Before signing the discharge summary, confirm:

  • [ ] AKI — if creatinine rose ≥0.3 mg/dL or ≥1.5× baseline at any point: document AKI with stage and etiology
  • [ ] Heart failure — if IV diuresis given, BNP elevated, or volume management required: specify systolic vs. diastolic, acute vs. chronic
  • [ ] Encephalopathy — if CAM positive, acute confusion, or altered baseline cognition: name the type and etiology (metabolic, toxic, etc.)
  • [ ] Malnutrition — if nutrition consult placed or supplemental nutrition started: document severity as physician diagnosis (mild/moderate/severe)
  • [ ] Morbid Obesity — if BMI is ≥40, or BMI is 35–39.9 with severe comorbidities: document "morbid obesity" explicitly, not just "obese" or BMI values
  • [ ] OHS — if patient uses home BiPAP or has known hypercapnia: document OHS explicitly, not just "morbid obesity"
  • [ ] Diabetes — specify type (1 or 2) and any complications (neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy); avoid "diabetes mellitus" alone
  • [ ] Anemia — if transfusion given or Hgb dropped significantly: document acute blood loss anemia (D62), not just "anemia"
  • [ ] Atrial fibrillation — if AF occurred or continued: document type (paroxysmal, persistent, long-standing persistent)
  • [ ] COPD — if bronchodilators escalated, respiratory therapy involved, or O₂ requirement changed: document acute exacerbation
  • [ ] Sepsis — if blood cultures drawn, IV antibiotics started, and clinical picture supports: document sepsis with source; do not leave as "infection" alone
  • [ ] POA status — confirm all secondary diagnoses reflect whether present on admission or developed during stay

Source: CMS MS-DRG V43.0 · FY2026 ICD-10-CM · Last updated June 2026

Payment figures are national averages; vary by hospital wage index. CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule.

/reference/shfft.title: TEAM Quick Reference — Surgical Hip/Femur Fracture Treatment (SHFFT)
/reference/shfft.html:
TEAM Quick Reference — Surgical Hip/Femur Fracture Treatment

DRGs: 480 (with MCC) · 481 (with CC) · 482 (without CC/MCC)

Tier structure: 3-tier — both MCCs and CCs move payment. Document both.

~Payment delta MCC → CC: ~$3,000–$4,500 · CC → base: ~$2,500–$3,500 (national averages; vary by wage index)

Post-acute context: ~38–54% of total episode cost occurs after discharge — the highest of all five TEAM procedures. Documentation gaps in comorbidities also affect SNF/IRF placement appropriateness and post-acute quality benchmarking.

Top 5 MCCs — Highest Payment Impact

#MCCWhy It's MissedICD-10
1Metabolic or Toxic Encephalopathy"Delirium" or "confusion" written instead — delirium is a CC, encephalopathy is an MCCG93.41, G92.9
2Acute Systolic or Diastolic Heart Failure"CHF" or "volume overloaded" — neither is an MCCI50.21, I50.23, I50.31, I50.33
3Acute Kidney InjuryCreatinine elevation documented as lab finding, not AKI diagnosisN17.0–N17.9
4Severe Protein-Calorie MalnutritionDietitian documents; physician doesn't — dietitian-only diagnosis is not codeableE43
5Sepsis"Infection" or "UTI" documented without systemic response languageA41.x + R65.20/R65.21

Also consider: Acute respiratory failure (J96.01), aspiration pneumonia (J69.0), acute pulmonary edema (J81.0)

Top 10 CCs — Payment and Quality Value

Clinical Note

In SHFFT's 3-tier structure, CCs directly increase DRG payment. Document all that apply.

#CCCommon MissICD-10
1Dementia with behavioral disturbance"Dementia" without behavioral specification; "confusion" onlyF02.811, F03.911
2Acute blood loss anemia"Postop anemia" or transfusion ordered without diagnosisD62
3Drug-induced delirium"Confusion" or "AMS" — symptom documented, not diagnosisF05
4Chronic systolic or diastolic HF (stable)"CHF" unspecified — no CC/MCC capturedI50.22, I50.32
5Moderate malnutritionNo physician nutrition diagnosis despite nutrition consultE44.0
6COPD with acute exacerbation"COPD" without exacerbation statusJ44.1
7Atrial fibrillation (specified type)"A-fib" without type; "irregular rhythm"I48.0, I48.11, I48.19
8Hyponatremia or hypernatremiaElectrolyte abnormalities documented as labs, not diagnosesE87.0, E87.1
9Hemiplegia / hemiparesis"History of stroke" without documenting current motor deficitG81.90–G81.94
10Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40)"Obese" or "BMI 42" written without diagnosis — Z68 code alone is not a CCE66.01

Key HCCs — Target Price Risk Adjustment

SHFFT has 16 HCC risk adjustment variables — the same count as LEJR. The admission H&P is usually the only HCC documentation opportunity for this urgent population. There is no pre-op clinic visit.

HCCConditionDocumentation Trigger
125/126/127Dementia (mild / moderate / severe)Name it and stage it — "confusion" fails; document pre-fracture baseline
224/225/226Heart failure (any type/acuity)Specify systolic vs. diastolic; acute vs. chronic
280COPDSeverity, exacerbation status, current medications
253Hemiplegia / hemiparesisActive neurological deficit from prior stroke — not just "history of stroke"
37Diabetes with chronic complicationsName the complication — neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy
267DVT / PEAcute or chronic; document if on anticoagulation for prior VTE
238Specified heart arrhythmiasAF type — paroxysmal, persistent, permanent
48Morbid obesityBMI ≥40 or BMI 35-39.9 with comorbidities + provider diagnosis

The admission H&P must do triple work for SHFFT: establish POA, capture HCCs, and set the comorbidity baseline — all in one document, written urgently. Treat it accordingly.

Exact Phrasing Examples

Morbid Obesity

Instead of: "Obese, BMI 36.5, history of diabetes and HTN."

Write: "Morbid obesity due to comorbidities (BMI 36.5, severe weight-exacerbated diabetes and hypertension) — requires customized postoperative mobility planning and respiratory monitoring."

Dementia (most common miss in SHFFT)

Instead of: "Patient confused, likely dementia per family."

Write: "Moderate Alzheimer's dementia (pre-fracture MMSE 14/30 per family). Behavioral disturbance — agitation present. On donepezil. Baseline cognition confirmed with family prior to fall."

Encephalopathy vs. delirium

Instead of: "Delirium, multifactorial — pain, sleep deprivation, unfamiliar environment."

Write: "Metabolic encephalopathy secondary to hyponatremia (Na 124) and uremia. CAM positive. Treating underlying metabolic etiology."

Clinical Note

Delirium (F05) = CC. Metabolic encephalopathy (G93.41) = MCC. Name the etiology.

Heart failure

Instead of: "Volume overloaded, CHF — gave Lasix."

Write: "Acute on chronic systolic heart failure. IV diuresis initiated, 1.8L net negative. Transitioning to oral Lasix. EF 40% on prior echo."

Malnutrition

Instead of: "Nutrition consult placed for poor intake."

Write: "Severe protein-calorie malnutrition — >10% weight loss over 3 months, significant muscle and fat wasting on exam, albumin 2.1. Meeting ASPEN criteria for severe malnutrition in the setting of acute illness. Enteral nutrition initiated."

Hemiplegia

Instead of: "History of stroke, left-sided weakness."

Write: "Left hemiparesis — residual deficit from prior right MCA stroke. Baseline ambulation with hemi-walker. Deficit present on admission and predates fracture."

Discharge Documentation Checklist

Before signing the discharge summary, confirm:

  • [ ] Dementia — if patient has known cognitive impairment: document type (Alzheimer's, vascular, Lewy body), severity (mild/moderate/severe), and behavioral disturbance if present
  • [ ] Encephalopathy — if acute confusion occurred: distinguish metabolic encephalopathy (MCC) from delirium (CC); name the metabolic etiology
  • [ ] Heart failure — if diuresis, BNP elevation, or volume management: specify systolic vs. diastolic, acute vs. chronic
  • [ ] AKI — if creatinine rose at any point: document AKI with stage and likely etiology
  • [ ] Malnutrition — if weight loss, muscle wasting, low albumin, or reduced intake documented: physician must name severity (mild/moderate/severe)
  • [ ] Sepsis — if antibiotics started for systemic infection with vital sign changes: document sepsis with source, not just "UTI" or "infection"
  • [ ] Anemia — if transfusion given: document acute blood loss anemia (D62)
  • [ ] Morbid Obesity — if BMI is ≥40, or BMI is 35–39.9 with severe weight-exacerbated comorbidities: document "morbid obesity" to capture CC (+0.4885 weight shift) and HCC 48
  • [ ] Hemiplegia/hemiparesis — if prior stroke with residual motor deficit: document the active deficit, not just "history of stroke"
  • [ ] Hyponatremia/hypernatremia — if Na <135 or >145 required management: document as diagnosis, not lab finding
  • [ ] Diabetes — specify type and complications; avoid "DM" alone
  • [ ] COPD — if O₂ requirements increased or respiratory therapy involved: document acute exacerbation
  • [ ] POA status — all secondary diagnoses should reflect whether present on admission; critical for HAC/pressure injury cases

Source: CMS MS-DRG V43.0 · FY2026 ICD-10-CM · Last updated June 2026

Payment figures are national averages; vary by hospital wage index. CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule.

/reference/spinal-fusion.title: TEAM Quick Reference — Spinal Fusion
/reference/spinal-fusion.tierStructure: Variable — 2-tier and 3-tier depending on DRG family
/reference/spinal-fusion.html:
TEAM Quick Reference — Spinal Fusion

DRGs: 13 families across cervical, thoracic, and lumbar regions; anterior and posterior approaches

Tier structure: Variable — some families are 2-tier (MCC only), others are 3-tier (CC and MCC). Know your DRG family before assuming CCs have payment value.

~Payment delta (3-tier families) MCC → CC: ~$4,000–$6,000 · CC → base: ~$2,500–$4,000

~Payment delta (2-tier families) MCC → base: ~$6,000–$9,000 (CCs have no payment impact)

Important Note

DRG 402 (Cervical Spinal Fusion without CC/MCC) has no MCC/CC tier — all cases pay the same regardless of comorbidities. For all other spinal fusion DRG families, MCC documentation is high value.

Top 5 MCCs — Highest Payment Impact

#MCCWhy It's MissedICD-10
1Acute Kidney InjuryCreatinine elevation described as lab value, not diagnosisN17.0–N17.9
2Metabolic or Toxic Encephalopathy"Confusion" or "altered mental status" documented — neither is codeable as encephalopathyG93.41, G92.9
3Severe Protein-Calorie MalnutritionDietitian assessment not followed by physician diagnosisE43
4Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome"Morbid obesity on CPAP" or "OSA" documented insteadE66.2
5Acute Respiratory Failure"Hypoxia" or "respiratory distress" documented — symptoms, not the diagnosisJ96.01, J96.02

Also consider: Sepsis (A41.x + R65.20), acute systolic/diastolic HF (I50.21–I50.43), vertebral osteomyelitis when fusion is for infectious indication (M46.2x)

Top 10 CCs — Payment and Quality Value

Clinical Note

Check your DRG family first. CCs move payment in 3-tier families; they do not in 2-tier families. All CCs have SOI/ROM and quality metric value regardless.

#CCCommon MissICD-10
1Obesity hypoventilation syndrome"Morbid obesity" or "OSA" — different diagnoses, different codesE66.2
2Chronic systolic or diastolic HF (stable)"CHF" unspecified — no CC/MCC capturedI50.22, I50.32
3Acute blood loss anemia"Postop anemia" without type; transfusion ordered without diagnosisD62
4COPD with acute exacerbation"COPD" without specifying exacerbationJ44.1
5Moderate malnutritionNo physician nutrition diagnosisE44.0
6Major depression, moderate/severeExtremely prevalent in chronic pain patients; rarely documentedF32.1, F32.2, F33.1, F33.2
7Myelopathy (when not principal dx)"Stenosis" or "weakness" instead of myelopathy diagnosisG99.2, M47.10–M47.16
8Diabetes with neuropathy"Diabetes" without specifying complicationE11.40, E10.40
9Atrial fibrillation (specified type)"A-fib" without typeI48.0, I48.11, I48.19
10Morbid obesity (BMI ≥40)"Obese" or "BMI 42" written without diagnosis — Z68 code alone is not a CCE66.01

Key HCCs — Target Price Risk Adjustment

Spinal fusion has 13 HCC risk adjustment variables. The population skews younger than LEJR/SHFFT but carries significant metabolic and psychiatric comorbidity.

HCCConditionDocumentation Trigger
72Spinal cord disorder / myelopathy"Cervical myelopathy" not "cervical stenosis with weakness" — the diagnosis, not the symptom
155/158Major depression (moderate-severe / mild)Highly prevalent in chronic pain population; name it, specify severity
37Diabetes with chronic complicationsName the complication — neuropathy is especially relevant for spine patients
48Morbid obesityBMI ≥40 with physician diagnosis; OHS (E66.2) separately if present
54Drug/alcohol dependenceActive substance use disorder — not "history of" if currently active
280COPDSeverity and exacerbation status at every encounter
21Bone/joint infectionVertebral osteomyelitis when fusion performed for infectious indication

Exact Phrasing Examples

Myelopathy (spinal fusion-specific)

Instead of: "Cervical stenosis with upper extremity weakness — proceed with ACDF."

Write: "Cervical spondylotic myelopathy at C5-C6 (G99.2), bilateral upper extremity weakness and impaired fine motor function, modified JOA score 12/18. Proceeding with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion."

Morbid Obesity

Instead of: "Obese, BMI 42.5."

Write: "Morbid obesity (BMI 42.5) — patient's severe obesity requires specialized surgical positioning, customized bariatric bed in recovery, and extra personnel for mobilization."

OHS vs. OSA

Instead of: "Morbid obesity, uses CPAP at home for sleep apnea."

Write: "Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (E66.2) — BMI 46, home BiPAP, prior ABG with pCO₂ 52 mmHg. Daytime hypercapnia consistent with OHS rather than OSA alone. BiPAP continued perioperatively."

Depression in chronic pain patient

Instead of: "Patient anxious about surgery, on antidepressant."

Write: "Major depressive disorder, moderate (F33.1), on escitalopram 20mg with partial response. Active diagnosis, being managed by PCP."

AKI after spinal fusion

Instead of: "Creatinine up to 1.9 from baseline 1.0 — likely related to NSAIDs, monitoring."

Write: "Acute kidney injury stage 2 (KDIGO criteria — creatinine 1.9× baseline), likely NSAID and contrast-related. NSAIDs held, IV hydration initiated, urine output monitoring in place."

Malnutrition in spine patient

Instead of: "Patient has poor nutritional status, dietitian following."

Write: "Moderate protein-calorie malnutrition (E44.0) — unintentional 8% weight loss over 3 months in setting of chronic pain limiting activity and appetite, muscle wasting on examination. Consistent with ASPEN criteria for moderate malnutrition in chronic illness context."

Discharge Documentation Checklist

Before signing the discharge summary, confirm:

  • [ ] Myelopathy — if fusion performed for neurological indication: document myelopathy as diagnosis (not just stenosis); specify level and neurological findings
  • [ ] AKI — if creatinine rose at any point: document AKI with stage and etiology (NSAID, contrast, hypovolemia)
  • [ ] OHS — if patient uses home BiPAP or has documented daytime hypercapnia: document OHS (E66.2), not just morbid obesity or OSA
  • [ ] Encephalopathy — if acute confusion occurred: name metabolic or toxic etiology; distinguish from delirium
  • [ ] Malnutrition — if nutrition consult placed or supplemental nutrition initiated: physician documents severity
  • [ ] Depression — if patient on antidepressant for MDD (not just pain): document MDD with current severity
  • [ ] Diabetes — specify type and complications; neuropathy is especially relevant in spine patients
  • [ ] COPD — if respiratory involvement during hospitalization: document exacerbation status
  • [ ] Substance use — if withdrawal managed during stay: document withdrawal diagnosis, not just "history of use"
  • [ ] DRG family check — confirm your procedure maps to a 3-tier DRG family before assuming CCs carry payment weight; check the DRG family navigator in the full procedure module
  • [ ] Anemia — if transfusion given: document acute blood loss anemia (D62)
  • [ ] Morbid Obesity — if BMI is ≥40, or BMI is 35–39.9 with severe weight-exacerbated comorbidities: document "morbid obesity" to capture CC (+1.4214 weight shift on 3-tier cases) and HCC 48
  • [ ] POA status — all secondary diagnoses should reflect whether present on admission

Source: CMS MS-DRG V43.0 · FY2026 ICD-10-CM · Last updated June 2026

Payment figures are national averages; vary by hospital wage index. CC/MCC designations update annually with IPPS Final Rule.
